catalogTitle: שושן פורים הוא תחילת וסוף נס של מגילה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the miracle of the Megillah begins and ends on Shushan Purim, and that the mitzvos of Purim are the Jews' weapon against Yishmael in the last stage of exile.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with two stories of tzaddikim whose Purim joy brought salvation: the Lubavitcher Rebbe's farbrengen before Stalin's fall, and Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam during a flood. He then brings the Ya'aros Devash that Vashti was killed on the night of Pesach, the yahrzeit of her father Belshazzar, and the Chasam Sofer that the Beis Hamikdash could be rebuilt right after the war on Amalek on erev Pesach. This explains why Shaul counted the people with Pesach lambs, and, with the Ruzhiner's words, why Shaul spared Agag and what Shmuel cried about all night. The kings timed their feasts for after Pesach, but the wise men told Achashverosh that the day was in fact Shushan Purim, so the Megillah opens and closes with Shushan Purim. From 'vaya'avor Mordechai' and the Akeidah he teaches that mesiras nefesh crosses the Satan's barriers, and closes that the Purim mitzvos defeat Yishmael today.

en: According to the Ya'aros Devash, Achashverosh's feast was timed so that its climax fell on Pesach, the night Belshazzar was killed.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the war on Amalek is to be on erev Pesach and the Beis Hamikdash could be built that same night, so the kings waited until Pesach passed before celebrating.
The wise men told Achashverosh that the day Vashti was killed was not Pesach but Shushan Purim, so the Megillah begins and ends with Shushan Purim.
The first miracle of the Megillah is the downfall of Nebuchadnezzar's house, and the Mashgiach calls it the main miracle of the Megillah.
Like Avraham on the way to the Akeidah, Mordechai crossed the Satan's 'water' with the cry 'hoshi'eini Elokim', and this gives Jews the strength to pass the barriers of the final exile.
The Mashgiach says the Purim mitzvos of tzedakah, reading the Megillah, the feast with wine and the gifts are the weapons that defeat Yishmael.

candidateTopics: war on Amalek on erev Pesach

title.en: The Purim farbrengen before Stalin's fall

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how, fifty years earlier, while Stalin was plotting against the Jews, the Lubavitcher Rebbe at a Purim seudah told a story of an old chassid who shouted 'hurrah' three times at an election, and shouted it with the crowd. Two days later Stalin was announced ill, and he soon died.

title.en: Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam and the broken dike

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the queen of Holland sent to Rabbi Elazar of Amsterdam when a dike broke, and was saved; coming to thank him she found him drinking and singing, and he told her that on Purim drinking does more than a year of Tehillim. He then speaks of the present seudah of Shushan Purim and the need for great salvations.

title.en: Vashti and her father's yahrzeit on Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ya'aros Devash that Achashverosh's feast fell on Pesach and that Vashti had an excuse: it was the yahrzeit of her father Belshazzar, killed on Pesach night, and whether it was a leap year decided the matter. The proof is from the piyut of the Haggadah, and the Mashgiach asks how the paytan knew it.

title.en: Why wait for Pesach: the Chasam Sofer

summary.en: Since kings counted their years from Tishrei, the Mashgiach asks why the feast celebrating that the Beis Hamikdash would not be rebuilt was held after Pesach. He brings Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's decree that the whole day of the omer waving is forbidden for new grain, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation: the war on Amalek will be on erev Pesach, and right after it the Beis Hamikdash can be built.

title.en: Shaul's war on Amalek and the Pesach lambs

summary.en: With the Chasam Sofer the Mashgiach explains the haftarah of Parshas Zachor: Shaul counted the people with lambs, which the Targum Yonasan says were the Pesach lambs, since the war was on erev Pesach. Leaving Agag alive while the war was still going on was not yet a sin, but once erev Pesach ended the time for wiping out Amalek had passed, and Shmuel cried to Hashem all night.

title.en: The Ruzhiner on Shaul and Agag

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ruzhiner's answer to the Chiddushei HaRim: Shaul left Agag alive one night so that Haman would be born, the Jews would have Purim and accept the Torah anew; but a king may not bring his people into danger. The Mashgiach adds that Shmuel's night of crying was a tefillah that Shaul's plan should succeed.

title.en: Shushan Purim opens and closes the Megillah

summary.en: Belshazzar and Achashverosh both counted from Tishrei but held their feasts after Pesach, knowing the Beis Hamikdash could only come after the war on Amalek on erev Pesach. When Vashti refused and Achashverosh asked whether it was her father's yahrzeit, the wise men answered that the day was not Pesach but Shushan Purim; the Megillah thus opens with Vashti's death on Shushan Purim and closes with Shushan Purim, and its first miracle, the end of Nebuchadnezzar's house, is its main one.

title.en: 'Vaya'avor Mordechai' and the Akeidah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara stresses that Mordechai crossed water when he went to gather the Jews. He brings the Midrash that the Satan turned himself into a river to stop Avraham on the way to the Akeidah, and Avraham cried 'hoshi'eini Elokim'; the Akeidah answered Yishmael's boast about his milah, and Mordechai crossed the Satan's water the same way, making Purim for all generations.

title.en: Ikvesa deMeshicha and the wine of Purim

summary.en: Bringing the Chiddushei HaRim that Purim sustains the Jews in the trials before Moshiach, the Mashgiach describes today's exile, with its politics, parties and elections, as a great 'water' meant to keep Jews from serving Hashem, and Esther's 'I have not been called' as the smallness of that time; the answer is tefillah with mesiras nefesh. He brings the Midrash that 'oil for the light' is Moshiach and explains that the Satan of Yishmael hates wine because his fall will come through the Jews' wine on Purim.

title.en: Esther's plea and the Purim 'breaking news'

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions a Slonimer custom of singing 'Vatosef Esther' and says this verse holds the whole strategy against Yishmael: to plead again and again, with more davening, learning and tzedakah. He closes with 'breaking news' that Yishmael has been struck down by the tzedakah, Megillah reading, wine and gifts of Jews everywhere, the final victory and end of exile, and asks for a niggun.

catalogTitle: חנוכה Can Bring Every איד Closer to the רבש”ע

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Chanukah lights carry the hidden light (ohr haganuz) and reach down even to Jewish souls that Shabbos cannot ignite, drawing every Jew closer to Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit for Chanukah, and brings the Me'or Einayim's reading: the soul is Hashem's candle, and some souls do not catch the fire of Shabbos, yet Chanukah can kindle them. He explains that the hidden light of creation, stored away for tzaddikim, appears in the Chanukah lights, is the light of Moshiach, and is present in every Jew as a hidden love that can never go out. He shows the same hidden light in Yosef and in Tamar during the Chanukah parshiyos. Because the Chanukah lamp is placed below ten tefachim, where the Shechinah normally does not descend, Hashem comes down to those who cannot rise. He then explains adding light each night, the name Chashmonaim, the one pure flask, and closes with Ma'oz Tzur, the exile of Yishmael and a tefilah for the geulah.

en: Following the Me'or Einayim, the Mashgiach reads the wicks and oils that do not light on Shabbos as souls that Shabbos does not ignite but Chanukah can.
The hidden light Hashem stored away for tzaddikim appears in the Chanukah lights and is the light of Moshiach.
Every Jew carries a hidden light, a hidden love for Hashem, like a pilot light that can never be extinguished, even in one who seems far.
The Chanukah lamp is placed below ten tefachim because on Chanukah Hashem comes down to those who cannot rise to Him.
Adding a light each night teaches that a Jew's avodah must keep growing, and Chanukah is the time to add fire to learning, davening and mitzvos.
The one pure flask the Greeks could not find is the point in every Jew's heart that can never become impure.

title.en: Wicks that Shabbos cannot light

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that inferior wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be used for Chanukah, and the Me'or Einayim's reading that souls are Hashem's candles. Some souls do not catch the fire of Shabbos; such a person should seek out a rav or tzaddik, but Chanukah can still kindle him.

title.en: The hidden light in the Chanukah lights

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Hashem hid the light of creation for tzaddikim in the Torah, and the Rokeach and other early sages that this light appears in the Chanukah lights. He brings the Midrash that it is the light of Moshiach, with which everyone will see Hashem in all of creation.

title.en: The hidden light in every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jewish soul is drawn to Hashem like a small flame to a large one, and that even a rasha has a hidden love, a pilot light that never goes out. The purpose of Chanukah is to bring this hidden love to the surface, which Chanukah can do even where Shabbos cannot.

title.en: Yosef, Tamar and the cheshbon hanefesh of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the hidden light in the parshiyos read around Chanukah: Yosef, whose brothers did not recognize him, and Tamar, who carried the light of Moshiach unseen by Yehuda. He then says every Jew should make a cheshbon hanefesh on Chanukah and bring out his own hidden qualities.

title.en: Below ten tefachim: Hashem comes down

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim, yet the Chanukah lamp is placed below ten. He explains that on Chanukah Hashem comes down to souls who cannot rise, which is why many Jews untouched by Shabbos still light Chanukah candles and feel close to Hashem.

title.en: Adding light, Chashmonaim and the pure flask

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that adding a light each night means a Jew may not stay on a plateau, and that the Greeks sought to abolish Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, to which Hashem added Ner, together spelling Chashmonaim. He urges adding fire to learning, davening and mitzvos, and explains the one pure flask as the point in every Jew that can never become impure.

title.en: Ma'oz Tzur, the exile of Yishmael and the Nesi'im

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the stanzas of Ma'oz Tzur, from Mitzrayim to the present exile of Edom, and brings the Midrashim that its last stretch passes to Yishmael and that the twelve Nesi'im read on Chanukah subdue Yishmael's twelve princes. He closes by saying Chanukah is a special time to daven for Moshiach and the geulah.

catalogTitle: צד א: אור המגילה יורד למדרגות הכי נמוכות ביותר.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, and that the Megillah, with its Targum Sheni, carries the light of kedushah down to the very lowest places, to strengthen the emunah of those who are far.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, which is why Kaddish is said in Aramaic: to subdue the sitra achra and reveal Hashem's kingship even among the shedim. Following the Arizal, Targum equals tardemah, deep sleep: holiness now seems asleep. The Megillah, unlike the Torah, descends to the lowest levels, and so it has a second Targum, just as Adar has a second Adar. He shows this in Esther's cry in the house of idols, in Shlomo Hamelech who went down into the strongholds of the sitra achra, in Esther sending a shed as her messenger, and in Yaakov leaving Lavan's last sparks for Gilad, the place of Eliyahu. Amalek's denial is answered by the Megillah's hidden miracles. He closes with an appeal for an organization that draws distant Jews close, and with the joy of Shushan Purim.

en: Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, and Kaddish is said in Aramaic to subdue the sitra achra and reveal Hashem's kingship everywhere.
Unlike the Torah, which begins on high, the Megillah descends to the lowest places, and therefore it has a second Targum.
Shlomo Hamelech dared to go down into the lowest places to reveal Hashem's kingship, and that is why so much of the Targum Sheni speaks about him.
Esther drew holiness down even into the house of idols, and even used a shed as her messenger, revealing Hashem's kingship even over shedim.
Amalek casts doubt into emunah by calling everything chance, while the Megillah, with no open miracle, teaches that everything is a miracle.

Esther and the house of idols

title.en: Targum, Kaddish and the back side of holiness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Targum is the 'back side' of holiness, close to the sitra achra, and brings the Beis Yosef that Kaddish is said in Aramaic to subdue it. Kaddish asks that Hashem's kingship be revealed even in the place of shedim, and Purim brings holiness down to the lowest point.

title.en: Targum as tardemah; Targum in Torah and Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal that Targum equals tardemah, deep sleep, and explains that holiness is now as if asleep; Avraham's prophecy came in tardemah and 'machazeh'. The Megillah goes down into the weekday world of Targum to give hope to the lost, and he brings the Gemara on where Targum appears in the Torah and in the Megillah.

title.en: The Megillah goes down: Targum Sheni and Esther's cry

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Megillah, unlike the Torah, comes down to repair the 'stragglers', and therefore has a second Targum, as Adar has a second Adar. He asks why Esther cried out when the Shechinah left her in the house of idols, and answers that she had to draw holiness down even there, as in our generation.

title.en: Shlomo Hamelech and the Targum Sheni

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shlomo Hamelech dared to go down into the strongholds of the sitra achra to reveal Hashem's kingship, which is why the Targum Sheni speaks about him at length. Shlomo ruled with wisdom, not war, as a mark of Moshiach ben David; the Megillah, rooted in Mordechai's Chochmah, reaches the lowest places, and Esther even used a shed.

title.en: Who carried Esther's words? A shed as messenger

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Manos HaLevi's question about who delivered Esther's answer to Mordechai, and gives his own answer: no one could know Esther was Jewish, as shown by her seven maids, one for each day, so she sent a shed. This explains the plural 'vayagidu' and why Mordechai had to go through water.

title.en: Yaakov, Lavan and the sparks left for Gilad

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that Yaakov spent his years with Lavan raising sparks of holiness, and asks why he left before finishing. He answers that the deepest klipah holds the highest sparks, which needed the power of Eliyahu at Gilad, where Yaakov also repaired the Targum 'yegar sahadusa'.

title.en: Bilaam, Amalek and the edge of the camp

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Bilaam sought to rule over 'ketzeh ha'am', those who had fallen outside the camp, like Amalek, and that the Megillah addresses exactly these, the level of Targum Sheni. Amalek casts doubt into emunah by calling everything chance, even the splitting of the sea.

title.en: Emunah at the Shushan Purim tish

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that Jews sitting at a Shushan Purim tish in the lowest of times is itself emunah: over a Megillah with no open miracle they bless 'she'asah nissim', which the Ramban calls the foundation of emunah. He ties this to Yaakov at Gal-ed and to the coming revelation that will end the sitra achra.

title.en: Drawing the distant close; the joy of Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks about an organization that draws distant Jews close, tells of bachurim in Eretz Yisrael it rescued, and says that one must daven daily for one's children in these dangerous times. He ends by calling to rejoice with Shushan Purim and the Targum Sheni, through which even the lowest give honor to Hashem.

catalogTitle: צד ב: במגילה נתגלה אורו של מלך המשיח

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai belonged to the world of the future redemption, beyond Ezra's level, and that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, by deriving the Megillah's holiness from 'u'zichram lo yasuf', grasped this light of Moshiach that is revealed on Shushan Purim.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the five days on which the Megillah can be read, corresponding to the five final letters, which the Midrash calls letters of redemption; the last, tzaddik, is the future redemption, and so Shushan Purim, the Purim of walled Yerushalayim, belongs to it. He then asks why only some of the Sanhedrin parted from Mordechai, and why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves the Megillah's holiness from 'u'zichram lo yasuf'. Through the Rambam's ruling that the Prophets will lose their force in the future but not the Torah and the Megillah, the Chasam Sofer's words on the Megillah, the eighth king Hadar whom Ezra recorded as dying, and the Ba'al haTanya's distinction between prophecy and wisdom, he explains that Mordechai lived in a world of the eradication of Amalek, above Ezra's prophecy. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, a special soul, grasped this, and it is the deeper light of Shushan Purim.

en: The five days of reading the Megillah correspond to the five final letters, letters of redemption; the last, tzaddik, is the future redemption, and so Shushan Purim, the Purim of walled Yerushalayim, belongs to it.
In the future the Prophets will lose their force before the greater understanding Jews will have, but the Torah of Moshe and the Megillah will not, and will be understood even more.
Each prophet wrote according to the level of his prophecy; Ezra did not reach the level at which the eighth king lives, so he wrote 'and he died' of Hadar.
Mordechai lived in a world where Amalek was already eradicated, and so he grasped what Ezra could not; Ezra recorded him as having fallen only because his book does not reach that level.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, a special soul, derived the Megillah's holiness from 'lo yasuf', likening it to the Torah of Moshe, and this reflects the deeper level of Shushan Purim.

title.en: Five days, five final letters, and Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the five days of reading the Megillah to the five final letters that the Midrash calls letters of redemption, and explains that the last day, Shushan Purim, is the tzaddik, the future redemption of walled Yerushalayim. He brings the Arizal via the Bnei Yissaschar on Haman and Zeresh drawing from these letters, and ties the gallows of fifty cubits to the fiftieth gate.

title.en: Mordechai, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, and what will remain

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why only some of the Sanhedrin parted from Mordechai, and why Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves the Megillah's holiness from the end of the verse, 'u'zichram lo yasuf'. He brings the Rambam that the Prophets will lose their force in the future but not the Torah of Moshe or the Megillah, explains what that loss means, and brings the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah reveals greater light than the Torah given under compulsion.

title.en: The eighth king, Ezra, and prophecy versus wisdom

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar on the parsha of the eight kings: the eighth, Hadar, has no 'and he died', yet in the book Ezra wrote it says he died, because Ezra wrote according to his level of prophecy. He then brings the Ba'al haTanya's answer about the Arizal grasping more than Moshe: wisdom can grasp beyond prophecy, though Moshe's prophecy is far greater, and nothing more can be grasped while Amalek is in the world.

title.en: Mordechai in a world without Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai was a soul of the time of Moshiach who lived in a world of the eradication of Amalek and so reached what Ezra did not. This answers why most of his brethren accepted him and why Ezra listed him as fallen: Ezra wrote according to his own prophecy, while Mordechai belongs to the world of the eighth king, above all those counted there.

title.en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and the two levels of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Chozeh of Lublin and the Satmar Rav rejoiced at a teaching of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and brings the Imrei Yosef's gematria for his name. He explains that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from 'lo yasuf' likens the Megillah to the Torah of Moshe and the secret Moshe placed 'in the ears of Yehoshua', and distinguishes Purim from Shushan Purim, closing with a blessing to see the redemption with our own eyes.

catalogTitle: מלכות של אסתר ע"י רוח הק'

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Esther's 'malchus' was ruach hakodesh, and that this was her answer to the Chachamim when she asked them to write the Megillah for all generations.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara in Megillah: Esther asked the Chachamim to write the Megillah for all generations, they feared arousing the envy of the nations, and she answered that it was already written in the chronicles of the kings of Madai and Paras. He finds this dialogue in the verses at the end of the Megillah and asks why the verse about Achashverosh's tax interrupts it. He rejects reading Esther's words as a queen's command: she always submitted to Mordechai and the Chachamim, and a queen has no such authority. Rather, Esther's malchus was ruach hakodesh, like the kingship of Shlomo HaMelech that will be revealed in the future Yerushalayim. Achashverosh, written without a vav, was a taker and not a true king; Mordechai and Esther were the true kings. He ends with Shushan Purim, the Kosel Maaravi in every Jew's heart, and a tefillah for Yerushalayim.

en: The Gemara's dialogue between Esther and the Chachamim is hinted in the closing verses of the Megillah: her request in 'umaamar Esther' and her answer in 'halo hem kesuvim'.
Esther did not press the Chachamim with a queen's authority; her 'malchus' was ruach hakodesh, and with it she revealed that the Megillah must be written.
Achashverosh was not a true king but a taker; the true kings of Madai and Paras were Mordechai and Esther.
Shlomo HaMelech's kingship over the upper and lower worlds came from ruach hakodesh and is a model of the kingship that will be revealed in the future.
The Jews of Shushan, who sinned more, received a greater day, Shushan Purim, because the inner point of a Jew, like the Kosel Maaravi, is never destroyed.

summary.en: Singing before the Mashgiach begins to speak.

title.en: Esther asks the Chachamim to write the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in which Esther asks the Chachamim to fix the Megillah for all generations and answers their fear of the nations' envy, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof that the Megillah was said with ruach hakodesh. He finds the dialogue in the verses at the end of the Megillah and asks why the verse about Achashverosh's tax stands between the question and the answer.

title.en: Did Esther speak with a queen's authority?

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gra, who explains that Esther spoke to the Chachamim with the authority of a queen, and asks: she always obeyed Mordechai and asked the Chachamim her questions, and a queen, unlike a king, has no law of obedience. He then notes that Achashverosh's name in the interrupting verse is written without a vav.

title.en: Malchus as ruach hakodesh: Esther and Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Esther's malchus means ruach hakodesh, as the Gemara reads 'Esther clothed herself in malchus', and compares it to Shlomo HaMelech, whose kingship over upper and lower worlds came from ruach hakodesh. Shlomo's rule without war is a model of the future Yerushalayim whose wall will be Hashem Himself, and the 'sixty mighty men' around him were, in the Midrash, sixty masechtos.

title.en: Achashverosh the taker, Mordechai and Esther the kings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Mordechai and Esther were the true kings and Achashverosh only an imitation, so Esther's answer about the 'kings of Madai and Paras' refers to their own kingship of ruach hakodesh. The interrupting verse sets this up: a Jewish king gives, while Achashverosh, who levies a tax, is a taker, and like Efron he loses a vav from his name.

title.en: Why the Jews of Shushan received an extra day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Esther's request for another day for Shushan: its Jews had an added sin, so even Purim was not enough for them and they needed a greater day. The love of Hashem hidden in every Jew, revealed on Purim, is a point that can never be burned, and Shushan Purim is Yerushalayim's day, when only Yerushalayim reads the Megillah as its Hallel.

title.en: The Kosel Maaravi in every heart, and a tefillah for Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'the city will be rebuilt on its ruin' as the Kosel Maaravi, which remains in every Jew's heart, and tells what he heard about the Satmar Rav's last drasha in Yerushalayim. He closes with a tefillah that all turn to Yerushalayim and soon see it surrounded by a wall of fire.

catalogTitle: מוסיף והולך - Striving for Greater Heights in עבודת השם

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that an oved Hashem is one who keeps adding beyond his own standard, and that Chanukah, with its candles that increase every night, trains a Jew to grow, to make every day a new beginning and to serve with mesiras nefesh.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk that in the days of Moshiach the difference between one who serves Hashem and one who does not will be seen, and brings the Gemara that one who reviewed his learning 100 times is not yet an oved, while 101 times makes him one, because he went beyond the standard. Chanukah, a taste of the days of Moshiach, teaches this through Beis Hillel's custom of adding a candle each night. A masmid who stops growing is no longer an oved. From Rashi's teaching that the mitzvos should be new every day, he explains Chanukah as chinuch, a daily new beginning. The Chanukah lights recall the Beis HaMikdash, making every Jew a kohen. The Rambam calls this mitzvah especially dear because it was won with mesiras nefesh; today, in the heels of Moshiach, every small act of self-restraint is mesiras nefesh. He closes with Chanukah as a time for healing barrenness in Torah and tefillah and for Tziyon.

en: An oved Hashem is one who does more than what is accepted as the standard; one who only meets the standard is 'lo avado', though he is no rasha.
Chanukah's candles, added each night according to Beis Hillel, teach a Jew to keep rising from one level to the next.
Once a person reaches a level and stops working to go further, he is no longer an oved Hashem.
Chanukah means chinuch: every day a mitzvah should be done with the freshness of the first time, like a bar mitzvah boy's first tefillin.
Chanukah is especially dear because it was attained with mesiras nefesh, and today every act of restraint against the yetzer hara is a form of mesiras nefesh.
Like Rosh Hashanah, Chanukah is a time when the barren are remembered, including those barren in Torah and tefillah, and Tziyon herself.

title.en: One hundred versus one hundred and one times

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk that in the days of Moshiach the difference between one who serves Hashem and one who does not will be seen, and brings the Gemara that reviewing 100 times is not yet service while 101 times is. He explains why the standard was 100 and why the extra time counts so much.

title.en: Chanukah's candles: adding every night

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Chanukah gives a small taste of the days of Moshiach and brings the Gemara's dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel on the number of candles. Beis Hillel's adding corresponds to 'do good', and the mehadrin who add each night live by the spirit of the oved Hashem who does more than the standard.

title.en: The masmid who stops growing

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a bochur who fights his yetzer hara and becomes a masmid learning eight hours a day, and asks whether he remains an oved Hashem once that is his routine; he answers that he does not, since serving means always striving for more. The same applies to sur mei'ra, such as extra care in kashrus, and he stresses that the time to work on this is now, before Moshiach comes.

title.en: Every day new: Chanukah as chinuch

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the mitzvos should be in one's eyes as new every day, illustrating with the excitement of a bar mitzvah boy's first tefillin. He connects this to the name Chanukah, chinuch, a new beginning, like the first day of the zman when a new Gemara is opened.

title.en: The home as a Mikdash, every Jew a kohen

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sfas Emes that the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Beis HaMikdash, and the Ran that one may not use their light, so the home takes on a glow of the Mikdash. Since preparing the lamps in the Mikdash was done by a kohen, each Jew becomes a kohen; to the Chasam Sofer's reading of the name Chashmonaim he adds that Chanukah spells 'kohen' and eight.

title.en: Why Chanukah is a cherished mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Rambam calls only the Chanukah lights a very cherished mitzvah, and answers that what comes through struggle and pain becomes dear, as milah was to Avraham Avinu. Chanukah was won with mesiras nefesh, when a few Chashmonaim went to war against the Greek armies.

title.en: Ikvesa d'Meshicha: the Satan's last meal

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites Rav Elchonon Wasserman's Ikvesa d'Meshicha and the Gemara at the end of Sotah on how hard keeping mitzvos will be before Moshiach. With a mashal of a condemned man's last meal he explains that the Satan, soon to be slaughtered, is now given unprecedented permission, which is why so many new inventions and temptations have appeared, to test who will be an oved Hashem.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh in small things

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that nefesh means one's will, so giving up a desire is mesiras nefesh, from giving one's life down to holding back. His examples are not looking at what one should not see, not making a hurtful joke in the lunchroom and not talking during seder; each is a tiny fraction of the Akeidah, and Chanukah is a time to check whether one serves by routine.

title.en: Chanukah remembers the barren

summary.en: The Mashgiach closes with the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah is like Rosh Hashanah, the day the barren were remembered. He explains that one who is not fruitful in learning or in tefillah is also called barren, lists the seven barren women ending with Tziyon, and calls on his listeners to daven to be healed of barrenness in Torah and tefillah and for Tziyon's children to return.

catalogTitle: מרדכי תיקן קצת חטא עץ הדעת

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains how Mordechai, by refusing to bow to Haman, repaired on the level of drush a flaw left by the sin of Adam and by Yaakov's bowing to Esav, bringing a tikun of the future world that makes the Megillah and Purim eternal.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Manos HaLevi: Mordechai's refusal to bow repaired Yaakov's bowing to Esav. The Midrash criticizes that bowing while the Zohar praises it; the Chiddushei HaRim resolves this through the four worlds matching sod, drush, remez and pshat, which Adam's sin set out of line. Yaakov chose a great tikun in the world of sod at the cost of a flaw in the world of drush. The Gemara's criticism of Devorah and Chulda shows a similar flaw: a time when men had to submit to women and din ruled over chesed. Adar is a reversed month, and the Purim miracle began with 'let every man rule in his house', the turn from din to chesed. Mordechai, from the world of tikun, repaired the drush flaw, which is why the Megillah becomes an iggeres on Purim, will never be nullified, and is expounded by the Gemara from beginning to end.

en: Mordechai, a spark of Yaakov's soul, repaired by refusing to bow to Haman what Yaakov did in bowing to Esav.
The four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, correspond to four worlds, and because of Adam's sin they do not always fit one another, so the Midrash and the Zohar can disagree.

A situation in which a man must submit to a woman, leadership through the attribute of din, is itself a flaw in creation; this, not the women's conduct, is the target of the Gemara's criticism of Devorah and Chulda.
The Purim miracle began with the first letters, 'let every man rule in his house', which set up a new order turning din into chesed, 'v'nahafoch hu'.
Mordechai came from the world of tikun and brought down a tikun of the future that did not exist even at Matan Torah, which is why Purim will remain when all else is nullified.

On Purim the Megillah is no longer one of the books of Kesuvim but an iggeres bound up with the world of tikun, and therefore it may not be written together with the other Kesuvim and will never be nullified.
Because Mordechai repaired the world of drush, the Gemara expounds the Megillah from beginning to end, which it does for no other book of Tanach.

title.en: Yaakov's bowing to Esav: Midrash and Zohar

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Manos HaLevi that Mordechai repaired Yaakov's bowing to Esav, then contrasts the Midrash, which criticizes that bowing, with the Zohar, which praises it. He resolves the contradiction with the Chiddushei HaRim: the four worlds match sod, drush, remez and pshat, Adam's sin set them out of line, and Yaakov chose a tikun in the world of sod at the cost of a flaw in the world of drush.

title.en: Devorah, Chulda and the order of honor

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Megillah that haughtiness does not befit women, shown by the unflattering names of Devorah and Chulda, and asks why only women, and what they did wrong at all. He lays out the order of honor between navi, kohen gadol and king, and how a king must stand before the kohen gadol who brings the word of Hashem through the Urim v'Tumim.

title.en: The flaw is the situation, not the women

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Chulda and Devorah acted correctly, since a prophecy and a judge appointed by Hashem's word demand that the man submit, as Tosafos explains. Following the Chiddushei HaRim he answers that the complaint is against the situation itself: leadership through din, a man submitting to a woman, is a flaw in creation, while chesed must be joined over din, as many halachos that give the right side precedence show.

title.en: Adar reversed and the first letters

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Adar a reversed month, citing the Bnei Yissaschar and the Arizal on its letter combination, in which din precedes chesed. The miracle begins with the first letters, 'let every man rule in his house': against Rashi's reading, which the Chasam Sofer calls forced, the Mashgiach explains them as the start of a new order turning din to chesed. Mordechai, of the world of tikun, brought a tikun never seen before, not even at Matan Torah.

title.en: Mordechai's tikun and the Megillah as an iggeres

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Yaakov: he knowingly left a flaw in the world of drush for a greater tikun in the world of sod, and Mordechai repaired that flaw, preparing the days of Moshiach. From the Rambam's ruling that a Megillah written with the other Kesuvim is invalid, he explains that on Purim the Megillah is an iggeres of the world of tikun, which is why it alone will never be nullified.

title.en: Doresh tov l'amo and Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Gemara expounds the whole Megillah, unlike any other book, because Mordechai repaired the world of drush, as its closing words 'doresh tov l'amo' hint. Shushan Purim is the Purim of Yerushalayim, written in the Megillah in its complete form, and Mordechai was beyond the grasp of others. He closes with a tefilah for the coming of Moshiach and the rebuilding of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Purim remarks on Haman and Amalek

summary.en: Another speaker makes light Purim remarks about saying Haman's name three times and how Amalek spoils the mitzvos of Purim, then introduces a rhymed song.

title.en: Rhymed Purim song on serving Hashem with joy

summary.en: A long rhymed recitation by another speaker, with a recurring refrain about taking joy from Purim, through vignettes of a Jew who keeps his good cheer through the trials of the year.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ו - שפע אור המגילה יורד כדי להחיות בן מלך

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the great light of the Megillah came down into the lowest places, like the Baal HaTanya's parable of the jewel poured out to revive the ill prince, in order to give hope to the Jewish people in a time of hiddenness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach discusses why Rav was displeased with a man who planted flax on Purim. Flax, the Pri Tzaddik explains, grows each stalk alone and signifies separation; it was Kayin's offering, while Purim gathers all Jews together. He contrasts Yaakov's household, called 'nefesh' in the singular, with Esav's 'nefashos', and explains through the Baal HaTanya that division comes only from bodies. He then asks why the Megillah, recorded in the Persian chronicles, did not bring darkness as the Greek translation of the Torah did. He tells how the Maggid fell ill over his teachings' writings lying on the ground, and how the Baal HaTanya's parable of a jewel poured over an ill prince brought him to recover. So too, the Mashgiach concludes, the Megillah's light descended into the lowest places to revive the prince, bringing hope to every generation.

en: Flax signifies separation, since each stalk grows on its own, and so planting it on Purim, a day of gathering all Jews together, displeased Rav more than other work.
Among bodies there is division, but among souls there is unity, so a person for whom the soul is primary can truly love every Jew.
Unlike the Greek translation of the Torah, which brought darkness, the Megillah being recorded in the Persian chronicles brought a great light.
Like the prince who could only be saved by pouring out the whole jewel, the highest Torah must be poured out to revive a very low generation, even if some of it falls on the street.

What happened to Esther, the soul of the Jewish people hidden in Achashverosh's palace, happened to the light of the Torah in the Megillah, which went down so low that Hashem's name is not even mentioned in it.

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rav was displeased with a man who planted flax on Purim. He brings the Midrash that Kayin's offering was flax and the Pri Tzaddik that flax signifies separation, the opposite of Purim, a time of gathering all Jews, and notes that flax was used only in the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Unity of souls, and the Megillah in Persian chronicles

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi contrasting Yaakov's 'nefesh' with Esav's 'nefashos', the families gathering on Purim, and the Baal HaTanya that division is only of bodies. He then contrasts the darkness that followed the Greek translation of the Torah with the Megillah written in the Persian chronicles, citing the Ibn Ezra, and brings that the highest holiness descended into the lowest places.

title.en: The Baal HaTanya's parable of the ill prince

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Maggid was displeased to see copied writings of his teachings lying on the ground and became ill, and how the Baal HaTanya answered with a parable of a king who finally let a doctor grind up the whole jewel of his crown and pour it over his unconscious son. The Baal HaTanya applied it to the high words of Torah that must be poured out to revive the Jewish people.

title.en: The Megillah's light poured into low places

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Maggid recovered through this plea, and applies it to the Megillah: its light, which the Chasam Sofer calls greater than the light of the Torah of Moshe, went down into Achashverosh's feast and the Persian chronicles, as Esther, the soul of the Jewish people, was hidden in his palace. Instead of darkness it brought 'light and joy', and the Mashgiach calls on his listeners to draw hope, bitachon and emunah from it and to thank Hashem.

catalogTitle: תשנ"ז - לעתיד לבא ישתלשל פורים בתוך תחום עשו

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim, a taste of the days of Moshiach, stops at the fifteenth of Adar because beyond it lies the border of Esav, and that in the future Purim will extend into that realm as well.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that the ten sons of Haman are read in one breath, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation: they were the ten forces of the side of impurity, each taking over when the one before fell, until all of it was nullified with Vayzasa. He then explains that Esther is likened to the moon, and the full moon falls on the fifteenth, so Shushan Purim, kept in Yerushalayim, is the deeper Purim. The Gemara asks why Purim cannot be extended to the sixteenth and answers 'v'lo ya'avor'; the Mashgiach explains that from the sixteenth the moon wanes, and that is the realm of Esav, who said 'lo sa'avor bi'. Purim is only a sample of the days of Moshiach. In the future, when the moon becomes whole, Purim will enter Esav's realm too. He ends with Mordechai stepping on Haman and the custom of stamping at Haman's name.

en: According to the Chasam Sofer, the ten sons of Haman were the ten forces of impurity, and only when the last of them, Vayzasa, was killed was the whole structure nullified; therefore they are said in one breath.
Esther is likened to the moon, and the moon is full on the fifteenth, so Shushan Purim is the essential Purim, and Yerushalayim, which corresponds to the full moon, keeps it.
From the sixteenth the moon begins to wane, and that diminishing is the power of Esav; the words 'v'lo ya'avor' mean that Purim cannot cross into Esav's border.
Purim is a level of the days of Moshiach, but only a sample of it, since the power of Esav still rules the world.
In the future, when the moon becomes whole, Purim will extend into the sixteenth and seventeenth as well, the realm of Esav.

title.en: The ten sons of Haman in one breath

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the ten sons of Haman are said in one breath, and the Chasam Sofer's explanation, built on how Moshe, Aharon and Miriam passed away: the ten sons were the ten forces of impurity, and only with Vayzasa was the whole structure undone.

title.en: Esther, the full moon and Shushan Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Esther is likened to the moon, which is full on the fifteenth, making Shushan Purim the essential Purim, kept in Yerushalayim, the place of the full moon. He asks why the Gemara's answer to extending Purim is the strange phrase 'v'lo ya'avor', and notes that from the sixteenth the moon wanes.

title.en: Purim stops at the border of Esav

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Purim a level of the days of Moshiach, yet only a sample of it. Esther asked for 'tomorrow' too, but she could not ask for the waning days, because they belong to Esav, who told the Jews 'lo sa'avor bi', and Hashem did not give them his land.

title.en: Haman's ten sons and the future redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'v'lo ya'avor' as Esav's cry at his border, which will fall when 'saviors ascend Har Tziyon to judge Har Esav'. He links the lower seven sons of Haman to the seven shepherds, and Vayzasa, the last, to Dovid HaMelech and Moshiach, so that the full end of Haman's structure is still to come.

title.en: Treading on Haman: 'midrach kaf regel'

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that in the future Purim will enter the sixteenth and seventeenth, and reads 'ad midrach kaf regel' as the footsteps of Moshiach. He tells how Mordechai stepped on Haman and answered him with 'v'atah al bamoseimo tidroch', Moshe Rabbeinu's last words, connects this to the custom of stamping at Haman's name, and closes with a wish for today's Shushan Purim.

title.en: The animals Yaakov sent to Esav

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Akeidas Yitzchak that the animals Yaakov sent to Esav were the souls of simple Jews, and asks what became of them; he suggests they went to Amalek and were the animals Shaul did not kill. He closes with brief remarks about the late hour.

catalogTitle: #1 A Beloved Mitzvah Because it was Acquired with Hardship

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvah of Chanukah is especially dear because Klal Yisrael acquired it with mesiras nefesh, and that its light carries kedushah into the darkness of night, the left side and the galus.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah is exceedingly dear, and notes that it is the last mitzvah the Chachamim instituted. He describes how the Greeks tried to impose their culture of strength and beauty and to uproot Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the mitzvos that show Klal Yisrael's chosenness, and how the Chashmonaim fought with mesiras nefesh. What is acquired through pain becomes dear, as with Avraham's milah and the Mishnah's cow, and so Chanukah is beloved. He compares the Hellenists to the Jewish Communists in Russia and the mesiras nefesh of today's returnees. He then explains the name Chashmonaim, the growing lights, and how Chanukah, lit at night, on the left and in the public domain at the tekufah of Teves, invades the realm of tumah, as Yosef's trial shows. Chanukah brings the Shechinah down to the lowest; he closes with the opportunity of this year, 5760.

en: The Mashgiach explains the Rambam's statement that the mitzvah of Chanukah is exceedingly dear: something acquired through pain and mesiras nefesh becomes dear to the one who sacrificed for it.
The Greeks sought to abolish Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah because these three mitzvos show the chosenness and distinction of Klal Yisrael.
The Mashgiach says the forces of kedushah and tumah are balanced so that there is free choice; night, the left side and the public domain belong to tumah, which is why most mitzvos are done by day.

Since the Greeks invaded the domain of kedushah, the Beis HaMikdash, Chanukah is lit at night, on the left side of the door, in the public domain, at the longest nights of Teves, carrying kedushah into the domain of tumah.
Unlike Shabbos, when a Jew rises toward the kedushah, on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down even below ten tefachim, so that even souls far removed can be kindled.
The Mashgiach says the year 5760 holds a special chance for the geulah, with Chanukah beginning and ending on Shabbos, and one should use it to produce kedushah to offset the forces of the year 2000.

title.en: The Rambam: a very dear mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah is exceedingly dear, notes that the Rambam says this of no other mitzvah, and explains that Chanukah is the last mitzvah the Chachamim instituted, completing the letters of the Aseres HaDibros that make up a crown.

title.en: The Greek culture of strength and beauty

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the Greeks sought to force their culture, the worship of beauty and strength, on the Jews, and contrasts it with the Jewish view, bringing the Gemara's story of the wise man and the queen's wine. He then says sports, which come from the Greeks, are nonsense whose heroes are often criminals.

title.en: Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and the mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Greeks targeted Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, which show Klal Yisrael's chosenness, and tells how the Chashmonaim fought with mesiras nefesh. Through Rashi on Avraham's milah and the Mishnah's cow that loves the calf it bore in pain, he concludes that Chanukah, acquired with suffering, is therefore the Rambam's 'very dear mitzvah'.

title.en: Hellenists then, Communists in Russia

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the Hellenist Jews who sided with the Greeks to the Jewish Communists in Russia, cites the Chofetz Chaim that a small army of mesiras nefesh would have won, and describes the return to Yiddishkeit today, including thirty teenage boys who underwent a bris in Russia.

title.en: The name Chashmonaim and the growing lights

summary.en: Building on the Midrash that Hashem answered Haman's envy of the Yamim Tovim with Purim, the Mashgiach suggests that Chashmon stands for Chodesh, Shabbos, Milah and Ner: the Greeks wanted to abolish three mitzvos and Hashem added a fourth. He explains that unlike every other mitzvah, Chanukah grows each night, a renewal tied to the word chinuch.

title.en: Kedushah and tumah: day and night, right and left

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Greeks invaded the Beis HaMikdash, so we invade their territory. He explains that kedushah and tumah are balanced to allow free choice, that night is the domain of tumah, as the passuk of the beasts roaming at night shows, and that therefore almost all time-bound mitzvos are by day, while kedushah is the right side and tumah the left.

title.en: Lit at night, on the left, in the public domain

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah is lit specifically at night, on the left side of the door and toward the public domain, which by the Zohar's explanation belongs to the nations, and on the longest nights of Teves. He explains the lunar and solar years and how the tekufah once fell on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, the time the nations make their holiday.

title.en: Nittel, the calendars and Adam's festival

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the minhag not to learn on Nittel and explains the two dates it is kept, through the Julian and Gregorian calendars. He then brings the Gemara that Adam HaRishon, seeing the days shorten after his sin, feared the world was returning to darkness until the tekufah, when he made a festival that later generations turned into an idolatrous holiday.

title.en: Yosef's trial on the tekufah and the letters of Yavan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that Yosef's trial with Potiphar's wife fell on a day of the nations' festival, explains that it was the tekufah, a day of no Torah learning, which made the trial greater, and reads 'kehayom' as the twenty-fifth day. Chanukah on the twenty-fifth offsets this by bringing kedushah into the long nights of Teves, growing each night, while the letters of Yavan show tumah spreading downward.

title.en: The Shechinah comes down to the lowest

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim, yet the Chanukah lights are placed below ten. Oils and wicks unfit for Shabbos are allowed on Chanukah, because on Shabbos a Jew rises up while on Chanukah the kedushah comes down; since the soul is a lamp, even those whom Shabbos does not reach can be kindled on Chanukah.

title.en: Two Shabbosos of Chanukah in 5760

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that this year Chanukah begins and ends on Shabbos, in a year he describes as having a great chance for Moshiach, which the nations mimic with the year 2000 and heavy missionary spending. He urges producing kedushah through learning, mitzvos and the Chanukah lights, and closes with the gematria of eight lights as 2000, offsetting the tumah of that year.

catalogTitle: ע"י הפור שהיפל המן נתגלגל נס של פורים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim is named for Haman's lot because Haman's casting of the goral aroused the world of the goral, where Klal Yisrael is judged by its hidden inner point, and so it was Haman himself who brought about the miracle.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why Purim carries the name of Haman's lot rather than of the salvation. Citing the Siddur of the Ba'al HaTanya, he explains that a goral is above reason and reveals the inner point of a Jew that only Hashem understands, as on Yom Kippur. Angels, as pure intellect, cannot grasp it, which is why Menashe's teshuvah came through a hidden tunnel. He then asks how the decree of the Purim era was annulled, and answers with the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching of several courts: the heavenly court ruled against Klal Yisrael, but Haman's casting of a lot aroused the world of the goral, where Jews are judged by their hidden love. This is a taste of the days of Moshiach, so Haman caused the miracle. He then shows that Jews, like terumah, can never be redeemed or exchanged, which is what Haman sought to deny.

en: A goral is above reason: it reveals the inner point of a Jew that only Hashem understands, which is why both Yom Kippur and Purim are tied to a lot.
Angels are pure intellect and judge correctly by reason, but the point of a Jew that is above reason cannot be explained to them, so Hashem accepted Menashe's teshuvah through a hidden tunnel.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, there are several courts above: the decree of destruction passed in the heavenly court of angels, but before Hashem Himself the Jews are judged by their hidden love, which never wanted to sin.
When Haman cast a lot to destroy the Jews, it aroused the world of the goral above, where no externality reaches, and there the Jews were judged by their hidden root, so the decree was annulled.
The whole salvation came through Haman's lot, since the decree itself came from the Jews' own sins; therefore the day is called Purim, after the pur.
Purim is a taste of the world to come and will not be nullified even when the other festivals are, because the inner point it reveals belongs to the days of Moshiach.
Jews are Hashem's terumah, holy in their very being, and can never be redeemed, sold or exchanged for another nation; Haman sought to deny this.

title.en: Mordechai, Moshiach, and Haman as cause of the miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the days of Mordechai and Esther the hidden root of every Jew was revealed, as it will be in the days of Moshiach, and that the nachalos of Eretz Yisrael were also given by lot. He concludes that Haman himself caused the miracle, since without his lot the first verdict would have stood, and that this 'v'nahafoch hu' is the point of the whole Megillah.

title.en: Ad d'lo yada, the circle of tzaddikim, and Purim's permanence

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'ad d'lo yada' through the inner point where all Jews are equal, like the future circle dance of the tzaddikim, and ties the goral to the fiftieth gate where the other side is subdued to holiness. He brings that Haman too had a spark, as his descendants learned Torah, and concludes that Purim is a festival of the world to come that will never be nullified.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude of about six minutes, with a mention of the verse 'v'ilu la'avadim v'lishfachos nimkarnu'.

title.en: Jews as terumah that cannot be redeemed

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi, who calls the opinion that terumah can be redeemed a mistake, and asks why Rashi speaks so sharply here. He answers from the verse 'Kodesh Yisrael laHashem reishis tevuaso': Jews are Hashem's terumah and can never be exchanged, and Haman's offer of ten thousand talents of silver was an attempt to redeem them, which is the opening of the Megillah's theme.

title.en: Tarshish, Amalek, and the eternal bond

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara singles out the stone tarshish, the stone of Asher, and explains that what has holiness in its very being cannot be redeemed; Haman, 'reishis goyim Amalek', the same gematria as tarshish, wanted the holiness to pass to him. He concludes that the Jews are betrothed to Hashem forever, an everlasting building that Haman could not undo.

title.en: A badchan's Purim rhymes

summary.en: A badchan, not the Mashgiach, delivers rhymed Purim verses in the Vizhnitz style, with questions on doubled words in the davening and the Megillah and stories, interspersed with singing.

catalogTitle: ע"י פורים זוכים לשושן פורים; מפלת המן ממדריגת חמישים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that keeping Purim properly lifts a Jew into the higher light of Shushan Purim, and that Haman fell because he tried to reach the level of fifty, the root of Jewish unity revealed in kriyas shema, which reaches down to the lowest Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Maharal: Esther wanted a greater Purim, on the fifteenth, when the moon is full, like the other Yomim Tovim. He tells how the Ba'al HaTanya's mezuzos were special only because the sofer wrote them on the fifteenth. Shushan Purim belongs to the walled cities and is earned by one's service, while the fourteenth came to the weaker Jews through the goral; one who keeps the fourteenth properly is raised into the fifteenth. He then turns to Haman, who, on Zeresh's advice, wanted to stop Mordechai's kriyas shema. Kriyas shema is emunah above understanding and the unity of all souls in 'echad', the level of fifty that Haman tried to reach and fell from, hanged on a tree of fifty on the day of the omer. That root reaches down to the last word of shema, to the lowest Jew, and this is the joy of Purim. He closes with why Purim was not extended to the sixteenth and seventeenth, and with Purim's power to lift a Jew from the dust.

en: According to the Maharal, Esther wanted Purim on the fifteenth, the full moon, the day of the month on which the Yomim Tovim fall.

The fourteenth was given to the weaker Jews through the goral, from a place no sin reaches; Shushan Purim is for the walled cities and is earned through one's service, and keeping the fourteenth properly leads into it.
Haman wanted to stop kriyas shema, which is emunah above understanding and the unity of all Jewish souls in the word 'echad'.
Haman fell because he tried to climb to the level of fifty, the place of Kodesh HaKodashim beyond understanding, and so he was hanged on a tree of fifty cubits on the day of the omer harvest.

The root of kriyas shema reaches down to its last word, 'Elokeichem', which stands for the lowest Jew in the last generation; even the suffix of Hashem's Name may not be erased, and Amalek, who tried to erase it, is himself erased.
The joy of Purim is that the Ribono shel Olam tells even the lowest Jew 'I am your G-d', binding him to Shema Yisrael.

Purim was not extended to the sixteenth and seventeenth because the waning half of the month belongs to Esav; when Moshiach comes, that border will be crossed, and the Gemara's question is in truth a tefillah.

title.en: The fifteenth and the Ba'al HaTanya's mezuzos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal that Esther wanted a greater Purim on the fifteenth, the full moon, like Pesach and Sukkos. He tells of a Jew who ordered mezuzos from the Ba'al HaTanya's sofer and secretly swapped them, and how the Ba'al HaTanya noticed.

title.en: From the fourteenth into Shushan Purim

summary.en: The sofer explains that the only difference was writing on the fifteenth. The Mashgiach explains that the fourteenth came to the weaker Jews through the goral, while Shushan Purim belongs to the walled cities and is earned; whoever keeps the fourteenth properly is raised into the fifteenth.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Zeresh, Bnei Brak and kriyas shema

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Zeresh's advice as a plan to stop Mordechai's morning kriyas shema. He suggests that Zeresh fled to Bnei Brak, where Haman's descendants learned Torah, connects the Arizal's spark of holiness in Haman to Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, and explains that the tannaim at the seder in Bnei Brak repaired that blemish of kriyas shema.

title.en: Haman reaches for the fiftieth gate

summary.en: Kriyas shema is emunah above understanding. Haman, the head of the klipah, wanted to leap from the forty-ninth gate of impurity into the fiftieth gate of holiness, and fell; he was hanged on a tree of fifty, the place of Kodesh HaKodashim, where all Jewish souls are one, the unity behind Esther's 'gather all the Jews' and mishloach manos.

title.en: Atika and the day of the omer

summary.en: Through kriyas shema a Jew attaches himself to the world of unity, called Atika, which no blemish reaches, as at the Yam Suf when Moshe was told not to pray. The Mashgiach brings the Maharal that Haman fell on the day of the omer harvest, the start of the count to fifty, and calls Zeresh's plan to stop kriyas shema on that very day foolish.

title.en: 'Ani Hashem Elokeichem' for the lowest Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the last word of kriyas shema corresponds to the left heel, the lowest Jew in the last generation, and that even a suffix of Hashem's Name may not be erased. Amalek tried to erase it and is therefore erased, measure for measure. The doubled 'Ani Hashem Elokeichem' is an expression of love, and the joy of Purim is that the lowest Jew is bound to Hashem.

title.en: Niggun

summary.en: Singing at the table.

title.en: Why not the sixteenth and seventeenth?

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that asks why Purim could not be extended to the sixteenth and seventeenth, answered by 'velo ya'avor'. Since letters after Hashem's Name are holy, days after Purim would seem more fitting; he answers from Esav's 'you shall not pass through me' and the promise 'until the treading of a foot', fulfilled at the geulah.

title.en: The waning moon belongs to Esav

summary.en: Holiness rises until the full moon of the fifteenth; after that the waning moon is Esav's portion, which is why weddings are not made then and why the war on Amalek cannot yet be carried into those days. In Moshiach's time it will, so the Gemara's question is a tefillah, and the sixteenth and seventeenth already carry the joy of hope in the geulah.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: Purim lifts a Jew from the dust

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chidushei HaRim that Chanukah and Purim hold the Jews in exile, and Rashi on Zeresh's words that Israel is compared to dust and to stars. Purim can lift even a Jew who has fallen to the dust up to the stars; the three-cornered hamantash shows this, and he closes with teshuvah from Purim on.

catalogTitle: ביאור ופירוש על פיוטי מוסף. ראשון לציון -חודש של גאולה

oneLiner.en: Through the Musaf piyut of Parshas HaChodesh built on the words 'Rishon l'Tziyon', the Mashgiach explains that Nissan is the month of renewal and redemption, given to the Jewish people who stand above time.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Musaf piyut of Parshas HaChodesh, whose stanzas begin with the seven words of 'Rishon l'Tziyon'. He contrasts Nissan, the month of chesed and renewal from which the Jewish kings count, with Tishrei, the month of din from which the nations count: the nations have only a 'shanah', a repetition, while the Jews have a 'chodesh', a renewal like the moon. Even a rose reddened by sin stays beloved, and the Jews, who sanctify the months themselves, stand above time, as the early redemption from Egypt showed. Nissan wakes the sleepers, for the heart of Yisrael, Hashem Himself, never sleeps. He explains why the hidden light of creation lacks 'vayehi ken', why Nissan brings salvation on credit and lifts even the lowest, how the spiritual rain of Nissan enters the matzah and the four cups, and closes with the hidden end, the four cups against the four kingdoms, and the four craftsmen of the redemption.

en: Nissan, from which the Jewish kings count, is the month of chesed and renewal, while Tishrei, from which the nations count, is the month of din.
The nations have only a 'shanah', a year of repetition, while the Jews have a 'chodesh', a renewal like the moon that is reborn after darkness.
Because the Jews sanctify the months themselves, they stand above time and set it, rather than being ruled by it.
Nissan wakes the sleepers: there is a point in every Jewish heart, Hashem Himself, that never sleeps and from which revival comes.
In Nissan salvation can come 'on credit', as the redemption from Egypt was granted on the merit of the Torah the Jews would later receive.
The spiritual rain that pours down in Nissan enters the matzah and the four cups, which carry Torah, emunah and blessing for the whole year.

title.en: The piyut 'Rishon l'Tziyon' and 'HaChodesh hazeh'

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the Musaf piyut of Parshas HaChodesh, whose seven stanzas each open with a word of the passuk 'Rishon l'Tziyon', because Nissan is the time of redemption. He reads 'HaChodesh hazeh lachem' both as Nissan being first of the months and as the mitzvah of sanctifying the new moon.

title.en: Nissan and Tishrei: renewal against repetition

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the two Rosh Hashanahs: Nissan, for the Jewish kings, the month of chesed and spring, and Tishrei, from which the nations count, the month of din. The nations have only a 'shanah', repetition, while the Jews, likened to the moon, have a 'chodesh', renewal, and like the bald man of the Midrash can shed their sins.

title.en: The red rose and a people above time

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the rose, even when red with sin, stays beloved and gives off a good scent, because the Jews stand above time. He brings the redemption from Egypt before the four hundred years and the mitzvah of sanctifying the month, through which the Jews set time themselves.

title.en: Waking the sleepers: the heart that stays awake

summary.en: On the stanza about waking those who sleep, the Mashgiach explains 'Ani yeshenah v'libi er': the heart of Yisrael, Hashem Himself, never sleeps. In Nissan the covenant of the Avos is renewed, every individual can renew himself, and Hashem hides the sins of the Jews.

title.en: The hidden light and 'lo ken haresha'im'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Midrash that the light of the first day lacks 'vayehi ken' because it was hidden on account of the wicked, and reads 'lo ken haresha'im' in this light. He notes that this Shabbos Parshas HaChodesh falls on the twenty-fifth of Adar, the day of 'Yehi ohr', and calls it a time to daven.

title.en: The chasimah, and Nissan at the center of salvation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the stanza must return to the theme of 'Magen Avraham' before the blessing's close, then turns to the stanza of 'l'Tziyon': Hashem hastened the redemption, and the precious light of creation shines from the twenty-fifth of Adar to Rosh Chodesh Nissan. Nissan stands between Adar and Iyar at the center of all salvations.

title.en: Salvation on credit

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'mekupos' as borrowing: Moshe asked in what merit the Jews would be redeemed, and was told they would receive the Torah, so the redemption came on credit. Nissan, the month of creation and chesed and head of the four seasons, feeds the whole year, and he prays that the hidden light made for Adam be renewed.

title.en: 'Zeh' and the month that lifts up

summary.en: On the stanza of 'hinei zeh', the Mashgiach explains 'zeh' as pointing at Hashem with a finger, as at the Yam Suf. Every Nissan brings a possible redemption, and even a Jew in the lowest depths is lifted up, since Nissan means to raise; the clouds then pour spiritual plenty.

title.en: Spiritual rain in the matzah and the four cups

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Nissan's mitzvos are mitzvos of eating: the plenty comes through rain into grain and wine, and per the Midrash grain is halachah and wine aggadah, so the matzah and four cups carry Torah for the whole year. Whoever opens his heart is filled, even if he feels like an empty pit.

title.en: Planting emunah in children; the Hallel of Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the young plants of spring to small children and says, citing sefarim, that the Seder night is the best time to plant emunah in them. He brings that the Hallel of Pesach 'cracks the roof' and that the four parshiyos, of which HaChodesh is the last, correspond to the four letters of Hashem's Name.

title.en: The hidden end, the four cups and the four craftsmen

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the end is hidden in Hashem's heart, that the four cups give the strength to be freed from the four kingdoms, and that if nature renews itself in Nissan, Klal Yisrael surely does. He closes with the Egyptians plowing over hidden Jewish children as a symbol of the exile, and the four craftsmen of the redemption.

catalogTitle: #2 Lighting the Candle of השם

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the empty receptacles of the Chanukah menorah stand for Jewish souls still waiting to be kindled, which will all be lit when Moshiach comes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the menorah has eight receptacles, most of them empty in the first nights, when a brachah should rest on fullness, as with a full cup for Kiddush and clearing empty dishes before bentching. To answer, he explains that Chanukah, unlike other Yamim Tovim, is by its very character a weekday. He then speaks of neshamos: the Satan snatches the finer souls away from their roots, and before Moshiach many return through teshuvah, as in the time of the Chashmona'im, who fought the Hellenized Jews and brought them back. Chanukah is a taste of Moshiach, which is why it has eight lights, eight being the number of Moshiach. Its candles belong in the reshus harabim, the Satan's territory, because a candle is a neshamah; each night another captive soul is kindled, and the empty receptacles are souls still waiting, until all are lit when Moshiach comes.

en: A brachah rests on fullness, so the Mashgiach asks why the brachah on the Chanukah lights is said over a menorah with empty receptacles.
Chanukah is a weekday not because it is inferior, but because that is its very character.
The Satan snatches the finer neshamos, and those who return in teshuvah are often more devoted than those raised in Yiddishkeit.
Chanukah is a sampling of Moshiach, and its eight lights reflect that eight stands for Moshiach.
A candle is a neshamah; the Chanukah lights are kindled in the reshus harabim to rescue souls held captive in the Satan's territory.
The empty receptacles are souls still waiting to be lit; on the 'eighth night', when Moshiach comes, all will be kindled.

title.en: Why light over empty receptacles?

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens on Kislev, the month of light, and asks why the menorah has eight receptacles that stand empty, when the Shechinah dwells in fullness and a brachah is said over a full cup and a cleared table. He adds that a mitzvah's depth is beyond us, but he will offer some insight into Chanukah.

title.en: A weekday Yom Tov and snatched neshamos

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Yamim Tovim, with special clothing and no work, with Chanukah, which is by its character a weekday. He then explains that the Satan snatches the finer neshamos in galus, that Moshiach will force him to return them, and that the present teshuvah movement already shows those who return to be especially devoted.

title.en: The Chashmona'im and eight as Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Hellenistic movement that drew away great souls, and the Chashmona'im's war against the Hellenized Jews, who were defeated and did teshuvah. Chanukah is therefore a taste of Moshiach, and he brings the Gemara that the Beis HaMikdash harp of seven strings will have eight in the days of Moshiach, so the menorah has eight lights.

title.en: Kindling captive souls in the reshus harabim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the reshus harabim is foreign territory, yet the Chanukah lights were meant to be lit there to bring kedushah into it. A candle is a neshamah, so each light rescues a captive soul; the empty receptacles are souls still begging to be lit, until all are kindled when Moshiach comes. He closes with the prayer for a new light in the brachah of Yotzer.

catalogTitle: “קול דודי דופק פתחי לי אחותי רעיתי שראשי נמלא טל”

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that in Nissan Hashem knocks on the heart of every Jew, 'kol dodi dofek... pischi li', opening the gates of blessing, and that the avodah of the month is to remove the chametz of the yetzer hara and take in emunah through the matzah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Nissan as the month of renewal, when the world was created and all of nature wakes from the sleep of winter in a kind of techiyas hameisim, because the Jewish people were reborn as a nation at the Exodus. Nissan brings down love, song and blessing, and each person chooses how to use them. The gates above open: Hashem knocks on every Jewish heart, 'kol dodi dofek... pischi li', bringing the tal of blessing. He explains the small aleph of Vayikra, matzah as 'patir', opening, the chesed of Nissan against the din of Tishrei, and the Chozeh of Lublin's pinkas. The avodah of the month is removing chametz, the yetzer hara, and eating matzah, the food of emunah. He ends with leaning on Hashem as the root of simcha, and with Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers.

en: Nissan is the month of renewal: nature's rebirth after winter reflects the rebirth of the Jewish people as a nation at the Exodus, and Nissan is a time of techiyas hameisim.
In Nissan the gates above and below open; Hashem knocks on each Jew's heart, 'kol dodi dofek, pischi li', because He comes filled with tal, the blessing of the month.
Nissan's guidance is chesed, in contrast to the din of Tishrei, so its avodah is through song, Hallel, matzah and acts of kindness.
The avodah of Nissan has two parts: removing chametz, which hints at the yetzer hara, and eating matzah, which brings emunah.
Matzah is 'the food of emunah'; its physical form is only a capsule for its spirituality, which is the same as the matzah eaten in Egypt.
Leaning at the Seder expresses that a Jew leans on Hashem; this reliance is the root of simcha, while sadness comes from having no one to lean on.
Pesach is the yom tov of Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, and the time to take in emunah and bitachon for the whole year.
