title.en: The Ramban's question on 'vehe'emin'

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties Pesach to the bris bein habesarim and brings the Ramban's question of what was great in Avraham's believing. He gives the Maharal's answer: by nature Avraham could have no children and he feared sin might undo the promise, yet he believed because Hashem wanted it.

title.en: Why 'Lech lecha' gives no reason

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Klal Yisrael began with Avraham and does not rest on merits. He asks why the Torah, unlike by Noach, gives no reason for choosing Avraham, and leaves his mesiras nefesh in Ur Kasdim to the Oral Torah: a Jew is a Jew because his soul is a part of Hashem, even when he sins.

title.en: The Ramban's 'great sin' of Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that Avraham sinned greatly by going down to Egypt and by Sarah being taken to Pharaoh, and asks how the Ramban could judge him so when even Korach and Zimri are judged favorably. He answers that the very first account after 'Lech lecha' shows a sin, to teach that a Jew remains a Jew and his sin is only external.

title.en: The Maharal: emunah is no small thing

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal's challenge to the Ramban and the Mechilta that the Jews at the sea merited ruach hakodesh for their emunah, and that one who takes on one mitzvah with emunah merits the Shechinah. He applies it: each Jew should take on one mitzvah with mesiras nefesh, such as a fixed seder after davening, illustrated by a story of a man who was 'dead' during his shiur, and Avraham withstanding the Satan at the Akeidah with pure emunah.

title.en: Emunah as firmness and foundation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says emunah is great even if it came easily, as a segulah, like the Midrash on oneg Shabbos. Emunah means firmness, like a peg in a firm place; Avraham is the rock from which Klal Yisrael was hewn, the foundation, and as he became the first Jew through emunah, the nation left Egypt through emunah.

title.en: A believer is subjugated to no one

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Maharal: one who believes depends on Hashem alone and cannot be subjugated, since subjugation is the opposite of existence; so the Jews, believing, became free and left Egypt. He brings the Maharal's explanation of why 'dog' is an insult in every language: the dog is wholly dependent on its master, a repulsive trait, while a person should depend only on Hashem.

title.en: Rooted in Hashem, always in simcha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a believer is rooted in Hashem like a tree planted by water, and answers the Ramban that emunah is a great feat, for even Moshe Rabbeinu fell short in it. He teaches that a believer is always in simcha, and tells the story of Reb Shimon of Yaroslav and his 'two cows'.

title.en: A believer never becomes angry

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that a believer does not become angry, since everything is from Heaven, as Dovid said of Shimi. Following the Maharal, Moshe's anger and striking the rock was the lack of emunah for which he was punished. He ends with the Midrash on Yaakov leaving Be'er Sheva saying 'me'ayin yavo ezri', a support for Jews in golus.

catalogTitle: צד א: במה אדע - עצמיות של כנ"י טוב; מדריגת אבות' שבטים' ושבעים נפש' גאולה עצם הגלות.

oneLiner.en: Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that a Jew's sin, and so his exile, is only incidental while his goodness is his essence, which is why Avraham was promised that korbanos would bring his children back to Eretz Yisrael and why the start of every galus already holds the geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Avraham's question 'bameh eda', 'how will I know that I will inherit the land', and asks how Avraham could seem to lack faith. Hashem answered: in the merit of korbanos. Bringing the Gemara in Megillah and the Midrash, the Mashgiach sets out the Maharal's rule: in a Jew sin is incidental, while in a gentile it is essential, illustrated by a man splashed with mud as opposed to one whose skin is dark. That is why a korban can wipe away a Jew's sin and draw him close to Hashem. Eretz Yisrael, a 'Jew in geography', spits out sin, yet it must return to the Jews, and this was Avraham's real question. The Mashgiach then distinguishes the avos, the shevatim and the seventy souls in their bond to Mitzrayim, and shows through the atbash calendar, Yocheved and Serach bas Asher that galus begins with the geulah already inside it.

en: According to the Maharal, Avraham's question 'bameh eda' was not a lack of faith but whether his children would return to Eretz Yisrael after being exiled for their sins.
A Jew's sin is incidental (b'mikreh) and does not cling to him, while a gentile's sin becomes part of his essence (b'etzem).
Korbanos, and today the saying and learning of korbanos, show that a Jew is close to Hashem and can be cleansed, and they protect the Jews in galus.
Eretz Yisrael is the 'separated land' that, like the Jewish soul, does not tolerate sin, and every nation has a land fitted to its nature.
The avos, the shevatim and the seventy souls are three levels in their bond to Eretz Yisrael and to Mitzrayim.
Galus for Jews is only temporary while the geulah is essential, so the geulah is rooted in the very start of every galus.

title.en: Avraham's question: 'bameh eda'

summary.en: Recalling that Avraham was the foundation of Jewish emunah, the Mashgiach asks how he could ask 'bameh eda'. He brings the Midrash that Hashem answered 'in the merit of korbanos', the objection of meforshim, and the Gemara in Megillah that korbanos would protect Avraham's children from the fate of the generations of the Flood and the Dispersion.

title.en: The Maharal's rule: sin by accident, not by essence

summary.en: The Mashgiach sets out the Maharal's rule that a Jew's sin is incidental while a gentile's is essential, with the mashal of a man splashed with black mud as opposed to a man whose skin is black. That is why a korban, which means closeness, can wipe away a Jew's sin, while a gentile may bring only an olah.

title.en: Korbanos and Torah as a shield in galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a korban accepted for a Jew proves his goodness is essential, while a gentile's good deeds bring no closeness. In galus, Torah, and especially the Torah of korbanos and the daily saying of korbanos, draws a Jew close to Hashem; he laments that yeshiva students treat saying korbanos lightly.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, a Jew in geography

summary.en: Every Jew must in the end become good, through whatever cleansing is needed, while gentiles cannot be cleansed. Just as the Jewish people accept no filth, Eretz Yisrael, the 'separated land', spits out sinners; the Mashgiach calls it a Jew by place rather than by soul, and touches on exile to the cities of refuge.

title.en: Every nation's land, and Avraham's answer

summary.en: Every nation has a land fitted to its nature, and Eretz Yisrael is the land of Klal Yisrael. The Mashgiach returns to the Maharal: Avraham asked whether his children would come back after being exiled for their sins, and the answer, korbanos, shows their sin is incidental, so they must return.

title.en: Avos, shevatim and the seventy souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes three levels in Klal Yisrael: Yaakov, who belonged wholly to Eretz Yisrael and was brought back there in full; the shevatim, branches of the tree, whose bones alone went up; and the seventy souls, Jews of galus who stayed in Mitzrayim. He brings a hint from sefarim in the word 'gevia', Yosef's goblet.

title.en: Who completed the seventy: Yocheved or Serach

summary.en: The Gemara notes that only sixty-nine are counted, and answers that Yocheved, born 'between the walls' at the border of Mitzrayim, completed the seventy. The Midrash says Serach bas Asher completed it; the Mashgiach asks how, since she is already counted, and explains she is counted as two. He then brings the Midrash linking the first day of Pesach with Tisha b'Av.

title.en: Pesach sets Tisha b'Av: churban rooted in geulah

summary.en: By the atbash rule the first day of Pesach falls on the same weekday as Tisha b'Av. The Mashgiach explains that Pesach, the day of geulah, determines the day of churban because a Jewish churban must be rooted in geulah; galus is incidental and geulah essential. So Yocheved, mother of Moshe Rabbeinu, was born at the very step into the first galus.

title.en: Serach bas Asher and Eliyahu, bearer of good news

summary.en: Every matter has an angel appointed over it, and Eliyahu Hanavi is appointed over good news. Serach, who told Yaakov 'od Yosef chai', took on Eliyahu's quality, so she lived on, entered Gan Eden alive and counts as two. She later confirmed Moshe as redeemer by 'pakod pakadti', and the Mashgiach concludes that the seventy souls entering galus already hint at the geulah.

catalogTitle: צד ב: ברית בין הבתרים - אדום הוא מציאות של שוא; החומריות נעלמת לפני מקבלי התורה; ביאור ענין ששבעים נפש כנגד שבעים אומות.

oneLiner.en: Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains the animals of the Bris Bein HaBesarim as the four kingdoms that Avraham's children will outlast, shows that Edom has nothing of its own, and explains why the servitude of Egypt began only once the Jews became seventy souls, corresponding to the seventy nations.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash that the animals Hashem showed Avraham at the Bris Bein HaBesarim stand for the four kingdoms, ending with Edom, a galus spread across many nations. Following the Maharal, the kingdoms are mere beasts before Avraham: he passes between them and they are cut apart, a promise that the Jewish people will outlive every obstacle, and each person carries these kingdoms within himself. The bird, Edom, was not cut at all, since it is a trifle; its greatness is robbed from Yerushalayim and from the Jews. The cutting also hints at the splitting of the sea, where physicality gives way before those going to receive the Torah. He then explains that servitude begins with Yitzchak, not Avraham, the root, and becomes real only once the Jews are seventy souls, opposite the seventy nations. Every Jew keeps the point of Avraham and the level of the shevatim, tied to Hashem's four-letter Name, which no galus can touch.

en: The animals of the Bris Bein HaBesarim are the four kingdoms, and the last of them, Edom, is a galus made of many nations.
The kingdoms are beasts compared to Avraham; they are cut apart as he passes through, a promise that the Jewish people will outlive them all.
The bird, Edom, was not even cut, because it is insignificant; all its greatness is robbed from the Jews.
The cutting of the animals hints at the splitting of the sea, where nature and physicality give way before the Jewish people.
Servitude could not begin with Avraham, the root of Klal Yisroel; it begins with Yitzchak as sojourning and becomes real only after the shevatim pass on.
Seventy souls correspond to the seventy nations; only at that level do the Jews have a connection with the nations, and therefore the galus began then.
Every Jew has within him the point of Avraham and the level of the shevatim, bound to Hashem's four-letter Name, which no nation and no galus can touch.

title.en: The four kingdoms at the Bris Bein HaBesarim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the animals at the Bris Bein HaBesarim are the four kingdoms: Bavel, Madai, Yavan and Edom. He describes Edom as a galus of many nations, which began in Rome from nothing and is hinted at in the 'melech goyim' among the four kings.

title.en: Beasts before Avraham, cut as he passes

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that the kingdoms are beasts compared to Avraham, obstacles that are cut apart as he passes, a promise that Klal Yisroel will outlive them. He compares the nation to a body whose cells are renewed, and adds that each person has the four kingdoms within himself.

title.en: The uncut bird: Edom the robber

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the bird was not cut, and explains with the Maharal that Edom is a small bird of no importance; its greatness is not its own but robbed. Its whole culture and progress are taken from the Jews, and likewise the yetzer hara's strength is stolen from the good.

title.en: Rome filled from the ruin of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tzor, meaning Rome, is filled only from the ruin of Yerushalayim, and plays on Yerushalayim written without a yud. He repeats that Rome grew out of the sea, from nothing, and brings Esav called 'small' and 'despised'.

title.en: The nation's birth and the splitting of the sea

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Bris Bein HaBesarim was the birth of the Jewish people, when its whole destiny was shown. He brings the Midrash that the cut animals hint at the splitting of the sea: before those going to receive the Torah, nature and physicality give way.

title.en: Why servitude starts with Yitzchak

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the four hundred years are counted from Yitzchak's birth, and explains that Avraham, the single root of Klal Yisroel, is above servitude. Yitzchak was only a sojourner, and even in the shevatim's lifetime there was no real servitude.

title.en: Seventy souls opposite seventy nations

summary.en: Using the image of a trunk, branches and twigs, the Mashgiach explains with the Maharal that seventy souls correspond to the seventy nations, and only at that level do the Jews connect with the nations and the galus begins. Yaakov and the shevatim only joined the count, so they were brought back to Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The point of Avraham in every Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the explanation of 'Magen Avraham': every Jew has a point of Avraham that many waters cannot extinguish, and no nation can enslave it, illustrated by the Previous Lubavitcher Rebbe facing a revolver. He then explains why the nations need borders while the Jews are bound to the inner, heavenly Eretz Yisroel.

title.en: The shevatim, the Name Havaya and Shevat

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the twelve shevatim correspond to the twelve months and the twelve combinations of the Name Havaya, to which the nations have no connection, unlike the seventy Names. A Jew reaches the level of shevet through his own chiddushei Torah, which are revealed especially in the month of Shevat.

catalogTitle: חנוכה Connects us to the אור הגנוז in the תורה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah, born of mesiras nefesh and completing the mitzvos of the Torah, holds the hidden light (ohr haganuz) concealed in the Torah, a light of eight that is above nature and points to Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rambam's unique praise of the Chanukah lights as a very beloved mitzvah. He explains that Chanukah came through the Chashmonaim's mesiras nefesh, and whatever comes with suffering is more precious, as Rashi shows from Avraham's milah and a mishnah about a cow and her calf; like the Akeidah, it is remembered by Hashem. Chanukah is also the last of the seven rabbinic mitzvos that complete the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, the siyum of the Torah's mitzvos. He then describes the ohr haganuz, which Adam enjoyed for 36 hours and which Hashem hid in the Torah, where tzaddikim find it, illustrated by a story of a Rebbe and a wealthy visitor. The 36 Chanukah candles carry this light. Eight is above nature, like the Jewish people's existence and the Torah, and on Chanukah a light of Moshiach appears, hidden in unexpected ways.

en: The Rambam calls the Chanukah lights a very beloved mitzvah because Chanukah came through mesiras nefesh, and what comes with suffering is more precious.
Chanukah is the last of the seven rabbinic mitzvos that complete the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros, so it is the siyum of all the mitzvos.
The ohr haganuz, the hidden light of creation, was concealed by Hashem in the Torah, where tzaddikim who learn lishmah can find it.
As the siyum of the mitzvos, Chanukah holds the ohr haganuz, and its 36 candles match the 36 hours Adam enjoyed that light.
Eight stands above nature, which was created in seven days; the Jewish people, the Torah and Chanukah's eight days all belong to this level.
On Chanukah a light of Moshiach appears, and Moshiach comes in hidden, unexpected ways, as shown in the parshiyos read before Chanukah.

Chanukah as the completion of the mitzvos

title.en: Why Chanukah is a beloved mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Rambam calls the Chanukah lights a very beloved mitzvah, a praise he gives no other mitzvah. He explains that the Chashmonaim went out with true mesiras nefesh, expecting no miracle, contrasts Avraham with Haran in Ur Kasdim, and brings Rashi that Avraham's milah was precious to him because it came with pain.

title.en: What comes with suffering is precious

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a mishnah in Shabbos about farmers who poured salt on a cow after calving so that she would cherish the calf born with pain. Chanukah, unlike Pesach, was itself the product of suffering, so it is beloved to Yidden and to Hashem, and like the Akeidah it is remembered for merit.

title.en: Chanukah as the siyum of the mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Chanukah to the Akeidah, the last test that sealed Avraham. He explains that the 620 letters of the Aseres HaDibros match the 613 mitzvos and the seven rabbinic mitzvos, the last of which is Chanukah, so Chanukah completes the Torah's mitzvos like a siyum or the completion of the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: The ohr haganuz hidden in the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the light of creation was hidden for tzaddikim in the future, and the Midrash that Adam enjoyed it for 36 hours, since Shabbos pleaded for him to stay in Gan Eden. Following the Zohar as the Ba'al Shem Tov explains it, the light is hidden in the Torah, and tzaddikim who learn lishmah see everything through it.

title.en: The Rebbe and the shortcut

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a wealthy man from America who complained to a Rebbe about his long walk to his office; the Rebbe told him of a shortcut in his own city, and when asked how he knew, answered that he looks at the whole world when he says Melech HaOlam in a brachah. The Mashgiach adds that what was once mocked, that every word and movement is recorded, is now seen in technology.

title.en: A glimpse of the hidden light; 36 candles

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that even ordinary people who learn lishmah sometimes catch a flash of a new insight in a Gemara, a reflection of the ohr haganuz. The 36 hours of that light match the 36 masechtos of Gemara, and since Chanukah is the siyum of the mitzvos it holds the light too, which is why the sefarim count 36 Chanukah candles.

title.en: Gazing at the candles; eight above nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a neglected minhag to sit by the Chanukah lights for the first half hour and gaze at them to absorb their kedushah and the hidden light. He then brings that the harp of the Beis HaMikdash had seven strings and that of Moshiach will have eight, and explains that seven is nature and eight is above it, which is why milah is on the eighth day.

title.en: A nation above nature

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Jewish people's survival, outliving every empire without a homeland, is above nature, and that the Torah, received after the seven weeks of the Omer, belongs to the level of eight. Every stage of the nation's growth, from the Avos to the 600,000, happened outside Eretz Yisrael, so Chanukah's eight days show the eternity of the Torah and a light of Moshiach.

title.en: The light of Moshiach comes hidden

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Rokeach that on Chanukah the light of Moshiach appears, and the Malbim that the eighth pasuk after seven of nature speaks of the Torah. Chanukah is a time to learn Torah in depth; shemen, oil, is linked to eight and rises above all liquids. He closes with Asnas, born from the episode of Dinah and Shechem, and with Yehudah and Tamar, to show that Moshiach comes in ways nobody expects.

catalogTitle: משה רבינו - עצמיות של תורה שהיא מקור החידושים; שכל נבדל - כולו רוחני; נשמה כוללת

oneLiner.en: Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu is pure form, a soul from the source of all renewal, set apart from the physical, and a soul that includes all of Israel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with Rashi's teaching that Yocheved became young again before Moshe's birth, and explains that Moshe comes from the higher world from which all renewal flows; his first mitzvah was Kiddush HaChodesh, and the Torah was given in the third month to show that Torah must never grow old. He then explains why the Torah does not name Moshe's parents: Moshe was separate from all physicality, and his redemption of Israel came from Hashem, not from his lineage, though the tribe of Levi is named. The name Moshe, given by Pharaoh's daughter as a reward for kindness, shows that he is form, the opposite of water, which is pure matter; this is why the astrologers tried to drown him and why he split the sea. Finally, he describes Moshe as an all-inclusive soul who cared for his brothers, passed three tests, and faced Dasan and Aviram.

en: Moshe's soul comes from the higher world, the source of all chiddushim, so at his birth his mother Yocheved was renewed and became young again.
Torah must feel new every day, and it was given in the third month, when the newness of the redemption would naturally have faded, to show that it must never grow old.
The Torah does not name Moshe's parents because he was separate from physicality and from ordinary family ties, and because the redemption had to come regardless of lineage.
Moshe is form (tzurah) and water is matter (chomer); therefore the astrologers tried to defeat him through water, yet form must overcome matter, as he showed at the splitting of the sea.
Moshe was an all-inclusive soul who felt his brothers' suffering as his own, unlike a lowly soul that does not care.
Whoever truly serves Hashem will meet opposition, as Moshe and Aharon faced Dasan and Aviram.

title.en: Yocheved renewed: Moshe, source of renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi's teaching that Yocheved became young again, and explains that Moshe comes from the higher world, the source of all chiddushim, which the world below lacks. He adds that Moshe's first mitzvah to Israel was Kiddush HaChodesh, and that renewal belongs to a Jew and not to a gentile.

title.en: Torah new every day; the third month

summary.en: From the pasuk of the third month and Rashi's 'let them be new in your eyes', the Mashgiach explains that Torah is always new, like the daily prayers that each open something different. Three times makes a habit, so by the third Rosh Chodesh the newness should have faded; the Torah was given exactly then to show it must never grow old.

title.en: Why Moshe's parents are not named

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal's two explanations of why the Torah does not name Moshe's father and mother: Moshe was a 'nivdal', wholly separate from physical ties, as his children also left no mark; and the redemption had to come no matter whose son he was. Only the tribe of Levi is named, since Levi, bound to Hashem, was never enslaved.

title.en: The name from Pharaoh's daughter; form and matter

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the Torah uses the name Pharaoh's daughter gave Moshe as a reward for kindness, and explains that the Torah itself is a Torah of chesed. He then begins the meaning of the name, 'drawn from the water', defining form as the spiritual, lasting essence and matter as its temporary garment, with water as the most formless substance.

title.en: Moshe, the opposite of water

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe is pure form, so the astrologers sought to defeat him through water, yet form overcomes matter, as at the splitting of the sea; only after the sin at Mei Merivah was he punished through water. Water is always plural because it has no single essence, while Moshe is unique; his merit even held back the Flood for 120 years.

title.en: An all-inclusive soul and three tests

summary.en: On 'Moshe grew and went out to his brothers', the Mashgiach explains that Moshe's greatness was his concern for others: a holy soul is a neshamah kelalis that feels another's pain, unlike a lowly soul. He brings the Chasam Sofer that Moshe passed three tests before being chosen to give the Torah: an Egyptian striking a Jew, a Jew striking a Jew, and injustice among gentiles in Midian.

title.en: A Torah for all; Dasan and Aviram

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe's Torah is for Israel and for all mankind, bringing the Rambam on the bnei Noach, and that Moshe did not give up doing good after a setback. He then teaches that whoever truly serves Hashem will face opposition, and explains that Dasan, from 'das', opposed Moshe the giver of Torah, while Aviram, 'the father is great', opposed Aharon's inherited holiness.

catalogTitle: משה רבינו - “ותרא אותו כי טוב” - אור הגנוז שנולד מהול

oneLiner.en: Building on the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised and filled the house with light because he was a 'separate form' with no share in evil, and from there he develops why holiness and blessing must always stay hidden.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash's readings of 'she saw that he was good' and the Maharal: the orlah is the power of physicality and evil, and Moshe, who had no connection to evil and came only to repair others, was born without it. Milah shows that man can improve on nature, as wheat becomes bread and grapes wine, which is why Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, brought Avraham bread and wine. The light hidden for the righteous lies under the orlah and is reached through toil, the work of Shovavim, until in Adar one sees that Torah is light. The Mashgiach then explains Moshe's name, the astrologers' error about water, and why Moshe married Tzipporah, a convert tied to the heavens like a bird. From Yisro's recognition of Sarah's modesty he concludes that holiness and blessing are always covered.

en: According to the Maharal, Moshe was born circumcised because the orlah is the power of evil and physicality, and Moshe had no connection to evil.
Some souls do not come into the world to repair themselves but only to repair others, and Moshe was such a soul.
Milah shows that man can improve on what Hashem created, like wheat that becomes bread and grapes that become wine.
The hidden light for the righteous lies under the orlah and darkness, and one reaches it only through toil and self-sacrifice.
Moshe, a 'separate form' equal to all of Israel, could not find his match within Klal Yisrael and married a convert.
The holier a thing is, the more it must be covered: the world hides Hashem, and blessing rests only on what is hidden.

title.en: Why Moshe was born circumcised

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash's readings of 'she saw that he was good', and the Maharal's explanation that Moshe was born circumcised because the orlah is the power of evil and physicality, while Moshe came only to repair others.

title.en: Souls that come for others; the Apter Rav

summary.en: Every Jew's life work is to remove the orlah, which begins with the bris. Tzaddikim who come only for others are spared the risk; the Mashgiach tells how the Apter Rav remembered being a king and a kohen gadol in earlier lives.

title.en: Milah, bread and wine: man perfects nature

summary.en: Milah shows that man can improve on nature, as in the Midrash's answer about wheat and bread. The Mashgiach explains why bread and wine get higher brachos, and why Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, brought Avraham bread and wine.

title.en: The hidden light under the orlah

summary.en: The house filling with light means the goodness of serving Hashem. That light, the 'light sown for the tzaddik', is hidden under darkness and obstacles, and is reached only through hard work and self-sacrifice, the meaning of milah.

title.en: Shovavim, Terumah and Adar: Torah is light

summary.en: The weeks of Shovavim are the time to remove the orlah, today through toil in Torah and tefillah. After them comes Terumah, where the aron (from 'or') shines, and Adar, when one discovers that Torah is light and milah is joy.

title.en: Moshe and water: form against formlessness

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that Moshe is a 'separate form' while water has no form, so water is his opposite. The astrologers saw that Israel's savior would be struck through water but did not understand that only his sin at Mei Merivah gave water power over him.

title.en: Why Moshe married a convert

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Moshe married Tzipporah, a convert, from whom a descendant became an idol priest. He answers that Moshe, equal to all of Israel, was not part of the six hundred thousand, so his match had to be someone else outside them, a convert.

title.en: Form and matter; Tzipporah the seventh

summary.en: Man is to woman as form to matter, and Moshe stands as form to all Israel; this explains why he was suspected regarding married women. The Torah notes that Tzipporah was the seventh daughter, since all sevenths are beloved, raising her to be Moshe's match.

title.en: Tzipporah: a bird tied to the heavens

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tzipporah's name shows her nature: like a bird, which belongs to the air and the heavens, her body was refined and fit for Moshe, who belonged to the heavens. The Midrash says she purified her father's house like a bird.

title.en: Yisro served every idol: the all-inclusive power

summary.en: Yisro served every idol in the world because his soul was tied to all powers and could rest only with the power that includes all, Hashem. This matches Moshe, who includes all Israel; like Moshe, Yisro had seven names.

title.en: 'Where is he?': Yisro recognizes Sarah's modesty

summary.en: The Midrash says Yisro's word 've'ayo' hinted that Moshe came from Sarah, of whom it says 'ayeh'. The Mashgiach explains: blessing rests only on what is hidden, and when Moshe did not come home to be thanked for rescuing the daughters, Yisro saw the modesty of Sarah's children.

title.en: The world as the Artist's camouflage

summary.en: As the Ba'al Shem Tov's students teach, all holiness is hidden: the whole earth is full of His glory yet He is not seen. Through the Gemara's 'there is no artist like our G-d', the Mashgiach compares the world to a painting and to camouflage that hides Hashem's trademark.

title.en: The holier, the more covered: Mishkan, Adar, head covering

summary.en: This world is a place where one must dig for G-dliness. The holier a thing, the more hidden: Purim and Adar, the Mishkan's coverings, the aron in the Holy of Holies, uncovered drinks, and the Jewish custom of covering the head, which the Mashgiach says has been weakened.

title.en: Hidden deeds and covered blessing

summary.en: Through Rebbe Reb Bunim on Lavan and Sarah, who did not come out for compliments, the Mashgiach shows that a Jew hides his mitzvos. Blessing is covered, like the challos at kiddush, and Adar is a hidden month until the reward stored for the righteous is revealed.

catalogTitle: A Time for הודאה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah, the time of hoda'ah, is a time of bracha in the sense of increase, tied to Yosef, to the number six and to Parshas Toldos, and he calls for real thanks and tefillah for Klal Yisrael in dangerous times.

abstract.en: Continuing from Mizmor l'Todah, the Mashgiach calls Chanukah the zman of hoda'ah, set for Hallel and thanks, and defines hoda'ah as awareness of receiving more than one deserves, as Leah felt at Yehuda's birth. After the story of the Maggid of Mezritch and the Ba'al HaTanya on how each sedra fits its week, he explains that Chanukah's mitzvah grows from night to night, which is bracha: increase, as the letters of the word bracha show. Yosef, whose name means addition, is the sixth and embodies bracha; Toldos is the sixth sedra, full of bracha, and Yavan is addition in tumah. The Mashgiach then speaks about the daily miracles behind Modim and Mizmor l'Todah, Kayin's and Hevel's offerings, the danger facing Jews in Eretz Yisrael and everywhere, and the need for tefillah, zechusim and teshuvah, since Chanukah is a time for yeshuos.

en: Chanukah is the zman of hoda'ah, set by Chazal for Hallel and thanks, and its gift for the year is thankfulness.
Hoda'ah is a person's awareness that Hashem gives him more than he deserves, as Leah said at the birth of her fourth son.
Bracha means increase, and Chanukah, whose lights and blessings grow each day, is entirely bracha.
Yosef, the sixth, is the embodiment of bracha, and the strength of Yosef is what earned the miracle of Chanukah.
Saying Mizmor l'Todah with thought is like bringing a korban todah, and saying it with one's mind elsewhere is like a flawed korban.
Jews in Eretz Yisrael and everywhere are in danger, and the Mashgiach says one must daven, gather zechusim and do teshuvah, since Chanukah is a time for yeshuos.

concern for Jews in Eretz Yisrael
reading of the Nesi'im on Chanukah

title.en: Chanukah, the time of hoda'ah

summary.en: Continuing from Mizmor l'Todah, the Mashgiach calls Chanukah the zman of thanks, notes that the Rambam puts the laws of Hallel in the laws of Chanukah, and explains that each Yom Tov leaves a gift for the year. Chanukah's gift is hoda'ah, the awareness of receiving more than one deserves, as Leah felt at Yehuda's birth.

title.en: The Maggid's ba'al korei

summary.en: The Mashgiach says each sedra is woven into the events of its week, and tells how the Maggid of Mezritch chose the future Ba'al HaTanya as his ba'al korei because he knew why each aliyah belongs to its day and to the person called up. He adds that Toldos is the first Shabbos of Kislev, the month of hoda'ah.

title.en: Bracha means increase; Yosef the sixth

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvah and the brachos of Chanukah are mosif v'holech, ever increasing, and that this is the meaning of bracha, shown by the letters of the word, each a doubling. Yosef, the sixth, became two shevatim, and his name means addition, so he embodies bracha, with the word bracha appearing six times in Yaakov's blessing of him.

title.en: All of Kislev is Chanukah; Toldos the sixth sedra

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the whole month of Kislev, the month of bracha, is Chanukah, which came from the mesiras nefesh of the Kohanim, like the readiness to give one's life in Shema. He then shows that Toldos is the sixth sedra, the sedra of bracha, with the word bracha in every aliyah, and ties Yosef to the sixth aliyah.

title.en: Yosef against Yavan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shelah that the strength of Yosef earned the Chanukah miracle, and explains that Yosef is addition in kedushah while Yavan is addition in tumah, invading what is not theirs, as the letters of the name Yavan show. On Chanukah Jews in turn go into the domain of tumah, lighting at night on the left side of the door; Toldos and the sixth aliyah carry the quality of Yosef.

title.en: Sixes of bracha

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the number six in Toldos: Yitzchak was sixty at the twins' birth and reaped a hundredfold in a year of hunger, and 666 is six in every place, the bracha of increase. Chanukah's thirty-six lights are six times six, the sixth aliyah holds the greatest bracha, Rosh Chodesh Kislev is the sixtieth day of the year, and the sixth middle bracha of Shemoneh Esrei is the one called bracha.

title.en: Daily miracles and the korban todah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Hashem makes miracles every day, so whoever thanks in Modim without believing it says something false. He explains why 'evening, morning and afternoon' was placed after 'Your miracles', that saying Mizmor l'Todah with thought takes the place of a korban todah, and contrasts Hevel's offering with Kayin's, which lacked a pure heart.

title.en: Caring about Jews in danger

summary.en: Bringing in his rebbe Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, who rebuked people for not caring what happens to Jews everywhere, the Mashgiach describes the danger to Jews in Eretz Yisrael, surrounded by enemies arming themselves, and in New York too. He recalls how in the war a German general's advance was turned back through miracles, and says that Hashem will make miracles but Jews must daven and not sit in apathy.

title.en: Chanukah, a time of yeshuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Chanukah is a time of yeshuos: the reading of the twelve Nesi'im on Chanukah is a zechus against the twelve princes of Yishmael. He calls for tefillah, zechusim and teshuvah, tells of a relative who wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael for America just before the Twin Towers fell, and brings the Gemara that a plague in Eretz Yisrael obligates Jews outside it too.

catalogTitle: התעוררות למצוות החג; מצה מאכל שהוא למעלה מן הזמן; קרבן פסח - בחינת אחדות ; מכת בכורות - בני בכורי ישראל.

oneLiner.en: Building on the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that matzah, the korban Pesach and makas bechoros all reveal Hashem's oneness, which stands above time, place and division, and he closes with a call to strengthen emunah and prepare for Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining that a Jew's eating is avodah, and that in galus matzah is the only eating left from the Torah; he speaks of the customs and chumros of Pesach, which he links to chametz being the yetzer hara. With the Maharal he explains that matzah is food above time: chametz is flour, water and time, while the exodus was above nature and time, which is why Nissan is called 'first'. He adds that chametz takes up more place than its truth, a false witness, while matzah testifies truly. The korban Pesach, eaten at bein ha'arbayim, roasted whole and in one group, shows Hashem's oneness. Makas bechoros struck the reishis of the klipah and revealed that every Jew is a bechor. A long discussion of the number two, the frog's song and R' Akiva's frog follows, and the Mashgiach closes on the signs of Moshiach and the need for emunah.

en: In galus, eating matzah is the only eating from the Torah that remains, and every food a Jew eats with the proper intentions is part of serving Hashem.
Chametz is made of flour, water and time, while matzah is a food over which time has no hold, because the exodus was above nature and above time.
Chametz swells and takes more place than its true substance, a false testimony, while matzah takes exactly its true size and testifies to Hashem's oneness.
The korban Pesach expresses Hashem's oneness: it is slaughtered at bein ha'arbayim, a time with no partner, roasted rather than cooked, and eaten in one group.
Makas bechoros struck the reishis, the first point, of the klipah, and so revealed that the Jews are Hashem's reishis and that every Jew is a bechor.
The number two is the power of division and tumah, which is why pairs are dangerous, why Seder Taharos opens with 'two', and why on Pesach night, a time of oneness, four cups are permitted.
The Mashgiach says the signs of Moshiach's coming are visible, and that the way to prepare is through emunah, toil in Torah and binding together with other yirei Shamayim.

title.en: Eating as avodah; the customs of Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's eating, with its halachos, intentions and brachos, is part of serving Hashem, and that in galus matzah is the only eating from the Torah left. He adds that after the churban the rabbinic mitzvos and customs grew in importance, and tells of a tzaddik who handed out kneidlach on the last day of Pesach.

title.en: Why Pesach is kept with chumros

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al HaTanya's ruling that on Pesach one takes on the chumros of the Rishonim, and tells how R' Yechezkel of Kuzmir hung his wheat from the ceiling. He explains with the Radbaz that the chumros of Pesach have no other reason than that chametz is the yetzer hara.

title.en: Matzah: food above time

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains why matzah must be made quickly: chametz is flour, water and time, while the exodus was above nature and above time. This is why the exodus had to be in the month called 'first', since the first point is not yet time.

title.en: Milah, Pesach and Hashem's oneness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that milah cuts a Jew off from nature, and the korban Pesach brings him into Hashem's oneness. Bein ha'arbayim is a time with no partner, the Pesach is eaten in one group, with matzah and maror together, and it is roasted, which draws a thing together, rather than cooked, which takes it apart.

title.en: Chametz, time and place: a false witness

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds his own point: if time has no place on Pesach, why is wine, which improves with age, central to the Seder? He explains that time and place are bound together, and that chametz is a false witness because time makes it take more place than its truth, while matzah testifies truly. Wine is from kedushah and carries the matzah's quality into the world.

title.en: The Pesach at night and the mashchis

summary.en: Following the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains why the Pesach is eaten at night: the night was the downfall of the klipah, while the redemption itself came in the morning. He then asks why the Jews had to stay inside if Hashem Himself struck Egypt, and answers that all destructive forces wanted to join in, so protection was needed from them.

title.en: Makas bechoros: every Jew is a bechor

summary.en: With the Maharal the Mashgiach explains that makas bechoros struck the reishis of the klipah and revealed that the Jews are Hashem's reishis, so that every Jew is a bechor. He then describes Nissan as the month of reishis and chesed, when everything begins to bloom, and a good time for a Jew to make a new beginning.

title.en: Pairs, four cups and the Seder each year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara in Pesachim that pairs are dangerous: two is the power of division and klipah, yet on Pesach night, a time of oneness, four cups are permitted. He brings Chad Gadya and the Rambam on the moon shown to Moshe, says that the exodus repeats every year at the Seder, and speaks of Shabbos Rosh Chodesh Nissan and the eighth day of the miluim.

title.en: How can impure animals sing shirah?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how impure creatures can say shirah. Through the Mishnah in Keilim on the sea-dog, which is impure because it flees to land, he suggests that each species has a pure counterpart that serves as its shliach tzibbur. The dog has none, and he answers that its tongue was made pure when it did not bark at the Jews.

title.en: The frog's song: Baruch Shem

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how the frog, a mixture of good and evil, can say shirah, and points out that in Perek Shirah it alone says 'Baruch Shem kevod malchuso', not a passuk, and quietly. This is a song that rises even from the places of tumah, and he explains with a Midrash that the mazikin flee when a Jew says Shema, saying Baruch Shem as they go.

title.en: The number two as division and tumah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the first day was 'one day', Hashem's oneness, while machlokes and Gehinnom were created on the second day. From this he explains the danger of pairs, the four cups at night, the Mishnah that ma'aseh merkavah is not taught to two, Yeravam's two calves, the two kinds of carrying on Shabbos, and why Oholos and Negaim, the gravest tumos, open with the word 'two'.

title.en: R' Akiva and R' Elazar ben Azaryah on the frog

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara where R' Akiva says there was one frog that bred all the others, and R' Elazar ben Azaryah tells him to go to Negaim and Oholos. Since those tractates open with 'two', the frog, a mixture of kedushah and tumah, cannot be called 'one' as a root; R' Elazar ben Azaryah holds it was one frog that whistled and the rest came, a partnership of one with many.

title.en: Shuruk, yesod and the weeks of Shovavim

summary.en: From the passuk in Zechariah and the Metzudos the Mashgiach shows that shuruk and kubutz are the same, a gathering, which corresponds to yesod, and with the Arizal he links the frog to yesod and the weeks of Shovavim to its tikkun. He says that in this generation the tikkun is not fasting but toiling in Torah and tzedakah, and tells how R' Yechezkel of Kuzmir told a penitent not to fast.

title.en: Moshiach is in the air

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the whole world is talking about Moshiach, and from Rashi on Leah he shows that what people say is a sign. He goes through the signs in the Gemara, especially that yirei Shamayim are mocked, and tells of a Jew in Detroit whose uncle called him 'meshuga frum' for keeping Shabbos.

title.en: An orphaned generation: Malachi's advice

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls this an orphaned generation with no one to rely on but Hashem, and brings Malachi's advice that the yirei Hashem speak to one another. Moshiach, greater than Avraham Avinu, will come suddenly, so one must prepare with emunah; from Pharaoh's words 'divrei sheker' he explains that the Jews in Egypt drew hope from talk of the redemption, and that waiting for Moshiach is a mitzvah.

title.en: Baruch Shem: joining ourselves to Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes today as a time when good and evil are mixed and serving Hashem is hard, and says each Jew must resolve firmly to stop stumbling and love Hashem even without desire. Yaakov Avinu, seeing the last generations, said Baruch Shem; from Sefer HaKanah he shows that its letters are the only ones that join with Hashem's name, and concludes that the advice is to bind oneself to those better than oneself.

catalogTitle: צירוף חודש ניסן - “ישמחו השמים ותגל הארץ” - חודש מלא חסד (פירושים על הגדה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nissan, whose letter-combination of Hashem's Name comes from "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz", is a month of chesed and renewal in which Hashem's kingship is revealed, and that the mitzvos of Pesach night, above all eating matzah and saying the Haggadah, plant emunah and draw down salvation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the renewal of Nissan: nature sprouts and sings because Hashem knocks on every Jew's heart, as in "pischi li" of Shir HaShirim. Through Vayikra's small aleph and the calendar he shows that Nissan reveals the love hidden in Adar. Pesach means opening, and matzah is the key that opens the heart. Nissan's letter-combination comes from "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz", followed by "Hashem malach": Nissan completed creation with the birth of Klal Yisrael and is the time of Hashem's kingship and of a judgment in chesed. The two central mitzvos are removing chametz, which is the yetzer hara and Amalek's doubt, and eating matzah, the food of emunah. Emunah brings true freedom and joy. Saying the Haggadah draws down the salvations of the Exodus, and the shiur ends with the final redemption hinted in the last day of Pesach.

en: Nissan brings renewal to the world: the sprouting and singing of nature reflect Hashem's love and kindness toward Klal Yisrael at this time.
The letter-combination of Hashem's Name for Nissan comes from "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz": the joy above is revealed on earth, leading to "Hashem malach".
Nissan is a time of kingship and of judgment in chesed, judged by Hashem Himself, in contrast to the judgment with din in Tishrei.
The two central mitzvos of Nissan are removing chametz, which stands for the yetzer hara and the doubts of Amalek, and eating matzah, which is emunah.
Emunah brings true freedom and joy: one who relies on Hashem depends on nothing else.
Saying the Haggadah is not only a remembrance: it draws down the salvations of the Exodus again for Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Nissan's renewal and Hashem's knock

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shabbos HaChodesh and the renewal of Nissan, when nature sprouts and sings. He brings "kol dodi dofek" and "pischi li" from Shir HaShirim: Hashem knocks on every Jew, His head full of the dew of blessing, and asks him to open up.

title.en: Vayikra's small aleph: Nissan reveals Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Vayikra, read in Nissan, is a word of love, written with a small aleph. Adar is a month of hiddenness when the aleph seems missing; through the calendar sign at-bash he shows that Nissan reveals what was hidden in Adar, that it was a call of love all along.

title.en: Pesach as opening; matzah as the key

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach is a time of opening, and that the Targum's word for matzah means opening; matzah is the key that opens the heart. Like two pianos tuned to the same key, Jews connect to Nissan's chesed by doing chesed, which is why Pesach begins with giving to the poor.

title.en: The letter-combination "Yismechu hashamayim"

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that Nissan's combination of Hashem's Name is the first letters of "Yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz": the angels' joy above is revealed below in nature and in Jews' song. The verse continues "Hashem malach", and he introduces the dispute whether the world was created in Nissan or Tishrei.

title.en: Nissan completes creation; Hashem's kingship

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the world was created in Tishrei in deed but in Nissan in thought, since Klal Yisrael, the purpose of creation, became a nation at the Exodus; this is why the first of the Ten Commandments mentions the Exodus. Nissan, the new year for kings, is when Hashem's kingship is revealed, while the nations were given Tishrei.

title.en: Kingship and a judgment of chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Nissan as the time when kingship is decided above and below, and when Hashem Himself will take over the kingship, which is why the redemption is tied to Nissan. He explains that the judgment of Nissan is greater than that of Tishrei but comes through chesed, as the straight order of the letters in "aviv" hints, in contrast to the reversed letters of Tishrei.

title.en: The Chozeh's notes and the two mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells, from the Bnei Yissaschar, how the Chozeh of Lublin wrote down in the first days of Nissan all that would happen in the year, and connects it to the verse about setting up the Mishkan on the first of the first month. He then explains that every mitzvah is a symbolic act that arouses above, and that all of Nissan revolves around two mitzvos.

title.en: Chametz, Amalek and the war against doubt

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why chametz has stringencies no other prohibition has, and answers from the Zohar that chametz is the yetzer hara. The main war with Amalek is on Erev Pesach; Amalek is doubt in emunah, rooted in bad middos such as pride, and today it spreads as heresy. Chametz must be removed before emunah can enter, a war that runs from Purim to Pesach.

title.en: Searching the heart; matzah is emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Lechovitcher sent a messenger to tell his chassidim to search the holes and cracks, and they davened Maariv for hours with great cries. He explains that one searches the heart as far as one can, then nullifies the rest and asks Hashem to remove it, and that matzah, the food of emunah, does this.

title.en: Matzah as a capsule; the freedom of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares matzah to a capsule that lets the body swallow emunah, and explains why the preparations for Pesach are so great. He brings the Satmar Rav that this whole night is matzah, and the Arizal that matzah equals three times Hashem's Name with its filling. Pesach night's freedom, he says, is the freedom of one who relies on his Father in heaven.

title.en: Leaning on Hashem: joy versus sadness

summary.en: From the Midrash on "vayasev" the Mashgiach explains reclining as leaning on Hashem. Simcha comes from being able to lean, while atzvus is the feeling of being abandoned, and idols are called atzabim. Avraham, the first believer, has his day on Pesach, and the emunah of Pesach grows from the first day to the last, which hints at techiyas hameisim.

title.en: Karpas, the Chasam Sofer and living with a question

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that karpas is done so the child asks, and tells how the Chasam Sofer let his son walk around with a question on emunah for days before answering, to teach that one can live with a question and still believe. In Egypt Jews nearly fell into the fiftieth gate of impurity; today that gate is heresy, and the main test before Moshiach is emunah.

title.en: The rasha, and the Haggadah as drawing emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the rasha denies the principles of emunah, yet today, since we have the Torah, even he can be rescued. The purpose of the Haggadah is to draw down emunah by speaking about it, and Pesach night is the time a father can plant emunah in his child. He brings the Targum Yonasan that on Pesach night the angels sing and the storehouses of dew open.

title.en: Haggadah from "gid"; the night that is day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haggadah comes from the word for a vein, which carries life, and from the word for mazal that flows down: saying it draws down. The night of the Exodus shone like a summer day, and the sages in Bnei Brak drew that light down until they did not know it was morning. From this he explains why Pesach night cannot be the source for mentioning the Exodus at night.

title.en: Drawing salvation: matzos, the Ropshitzer and the plagues

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Haggadah draws down the miracles of the Exodus again. He tells how the Ropshitzer, during the war between Napoleon and Russia, threw matzos into the oven on Erev Pesach to affect the war, and that Avraham prepared for his war by baking matzos. Each plague recalled draws salvation for Jews, and later generations expounded more plagues because more salvation is needed.

title.en: Rabbi Eliezer's four and Rabbi Akiva's five

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rabbi Eliezer counted four plagues in each plague and Rabbi Akiva five. Through the Gemara in Menachos about Moshe watching Rabbi Akiva expound the crowns of the letters, he explains that Rabbi Eliezer, linked to Moshe's soul, drew from the four letters of Hashem's Name, while Rabbi Akiva drew from the crown above them.

title.en: The last day of Pesach and the final song

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the haftarah of Beshalach, Devorah's song after a salvation that lasted forty years, with the haftarah of Pesach, David's song that ends with the eternal salvation of Moshiach. A new feminine song gives birth to further salvations, while the final one is masculine. He ends with the last day of Pesach, Moshiach's light and the hope that this be the last Pesach in exile.

catalogTitle: הלכות והתעוררות באפיית מצה בקדושה ובזריזות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that matzah, the 'food of emunah', binds a Jew to Hashem as chametz cuts him off, and urges that it be baked with zerizus, kedushah and every hiddur, with tefillah for success.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the joy with which Jews bake matzah and with 'ushmartem es hamatzos': zerizus is the very core of this mitzvah, and from it Chazal learn zerizus for all mitzvos. Matzah is the Zohar's 'food of emunah'; Pesach is the head of the festivals, tied to Avraham Avinu, the head of emunah, and the night of telling over yetzias Mitzrayim, the root of the whole Torah. Since eating matzah is almost the only eating-mitzvah left in galus, it must be done with every hiddur. In spring, when everything sprouts, the Seder night opens the blessings of Torah and yiras Shamayim. He then turns to practical concerns in today's bakeries: hired workers, clean hands and clothes, talking and spitting, eating chametz during breaks, sleeves, nails, cold water, and saying 'l'shem matzas mitzvah' aloud. He praises chaburos of ehrliche Yidden who bake with mikvah and kedushah, tells stories of tzaddikim's sensitivity, explains through the Radbaz that chametz is the yetzer hara, and closes with a story showing that one must also pray for a kosher Pesach.

en: From 'ushmartem es hamatzos' the Mashgiach teaches that zerizus is part of the essence of baking matzah, and from it Chazal learn zerizus for every mitzvah.
Matzah is the 'food of emunah'; the matzah one sees is only a capsule, and inside it is emunah, the root of all the mitzvos.
Since matzah is almost the only mitzvah of eating left in galus, it must be baked with every hiddur and great effort.
Matzah must be baked lishmah by Yidden who care about it; matzah baked by hired workers without mesorah, or by machine, lacks this.
Chametz is the yetzer hara that cuts a Jew off from Hashem, while kosher matzah binds him to Hashem.
Beyond all the care, one must pray and give tzedakah to merit kosher matzah and a kosher Pesach.

title.en: Zerizus and the food of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the joy of baking matzah and the custom of drawing the water with joy, then teaches from 'ushmartem es hamatzos' that zerizus is the core of this mitzvah. Matzah is the Zohar's 'food of emunah', like a capsule holding medicine, and Pesach, head of the festivals, is tied to Avraham Avinu, head of emunah.

title.en: Avraham's matzos and Pesach as the festival of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Avraham Avinu baked matzos and that all his successes came on Pesach, because Pesach instills emunah through the telling of yetzias Mitzrayim over the matzah. Emunah is the first of the Ten Commandments and the root of all mitzvos, so matzah teaches about all the mitzvos.

title.en: The last eating-mitzvah and the blessings of Nissan

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites a sefer that protests careless matzah baking: in galus matzah is almost the only mitzvah of eating left, so it needs every hiddur. In spring, when all of nature sprouts, the Seder night opens the blessings of Torah, halachah and yiras Shamayim, and he urges a matzah with all hiddurim rather than relying on generic brands.

title.en: A hard mitzvah: zechus, tefillah and lishmah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says matzah is a hard mitzvah to fulfil properly and one needs a zechus, tefillah and tzedakah to merit good matzah. He describes market matzah baked by hired workers without mesorah, the need for clean hands every eighteen minutes, and stresses that matzah must be baked lishmah by Yidden who care.

title.en: The oven worker, clean clothes and talking

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a visit to a bakery where the oven worker was the company's regular employee, which troubled him. He brings from the poskim that one should brush off clothes after eating before baking, and warns that talking while baking can lead to spitting a crumb of chametz onto the matzah.

title.en: Breaks, sleeves, nails and cold water

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks that those who stay to the end of the baking not eat chametz during the break, but rather Pesach matzah or egg matzah, mentioning briefly that the poskim disagreed about such matzos. He then discusses sleeves rubbing old dough onto new matzos, cutting nails, washing in cold water, and blood from the hands, which makes dough chametz at once.

title.en: Keeping cool and the power of speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the Chasam Sofer's marble tables and urges keeping everything as cold as possible, not keeping rolling pins near the oven, and not banging the sticks, which makes cracks that hold dough. He then explains the great power of a Jew's speech, as with hekdesh, and therefore one should say aloud 'l'shem matzas mitzvah' when baking.

title.en: Saying lishmah, again and again

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that a house built aloud for avodah zarah is struck with tzaraas, and the Bnei Yissaschar that the generation of the dispersion repeated 'havah' to strengthen their intent; so too one should say 'l'shem mitzvah' many times. He explains why machine matzos are not used at the Seder, praises the bochurim's baking, and notes that galus has weakened certain mitzvos, but Hashem accepts what Yidden do.

title.en: Chaburos, mikvah and the sense of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach welcomes chaburos of ehrliche Yidden who bake their own matzos, and mentions the practice of going to mikvah before baking. He tells of a talmid of the Lechovitcher who would not eat meat because the shochet had not gone to mikvah, and of Rav Avraham of Slonim who sensed that plates were not toveled, and brings the Mishnah in Chagigah on levels of purity.

title.en: Matzah binds, chametz cuts off

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one should avoid idle talk and leitzanus while baking, since matzah absorbs what is said over it. Matzah must be guarded from thieves, the forces of the Satan; chametz cuts a Jew off from Hashem and matzah binds him. He brings the Radbaz, who explains the great strictness of chametz in that chametz is the yetzer hara.

title.en: Chumros of Pesach and the need for tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Vizhnitzer Rebbe's fervor at bedikas chametz, says one must not mock those with chumros on Pesach, citing the Bnei Yissaschar, and tells a story from the Satmar Rav of a tzaddik who found wheat in his soup despite all his care and was answered from Heaven that he had not prayed. He closes asking that people give tzedakah and pray before baking, with a brachah for a kosher and joyous Pesach.

catalogTitle: The Greek War Against Faithfulness

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Greek war against Klal Yisrael was a war against emunah, which is faithfulness, the bond of Klal Yisrael to Hashem like a wife to her husband, and that tumah is what breaks that bond.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the principle that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children: the episode of Dina and Shechem foreshadows the Greek decrees, and Levi, not Shimon, led the fight, as the Kohanim and Yehudis did at Chanukah. He asks why, according to the Rashbam, the women were the main part of the miracle. Greek philosophy accepts only what the mind understands; emunah is faithfulness, an instinctive bond like that of a wife to her husband, which the Avnei Nezer uses to explain why a woman is trusted to remarry on one witness. The name Yisrael expresses that bond, and tumah is a barrier that destroys it, so the Greeks set out to defile. The pach shemen came from the place where the dust for the sotah was taken. Yaakov needed the name Yisrael before facing Shechem. The Mashgiach ends with today's war of tumah brought in through electronic devices.

en: The episode of Dina and Shechem was a sign for the Greek decrees, and Levi and the Kohanim, not Shimon, were the ones who won that war.
Greek philosophy accepts only what the mind can understand and prove, which is the opposite of emunah.
Emunah is faithfulness: an instinctive bond between Klal Yisrael and Hashem, like that of a wife to her husband.
Tumah is a barrier that destroys that bond, so the Greek war against emunah was a war of tumah against taharah.
The Greeks tried to erase the name Yisrael, which expresses Klal Yisrael's bond with Hashem, and Yaakov needed that name before his encounter with Shechem.
The Mashgiach says the war of Yavan is being replayed today through tumah that enters Jewish homes, and calls for mesirus nefesh against it.

title.en: Dina, Levi and the women of Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban's principle that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children: the episode of Dina foreshadows the Greek decrees, and Levi, not Shimon, carried the fight, as the Kohanim and Yehudis did later. He brings the Rashbam that the women were the main part of the miracle and asks why.

title.en: Greek philosophy versus emunah as faithfulness

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the Greek idea of accepting only what the mind understands, shows its illogic with an example from medicine, and defines emunah as faithfulness, an instinctive bond like a wife's to her husband. He brings the Avnei Nezer on why a woman may remarry on one witness, and explains that Levi felt this bond more, rallying to 'Mi laShem elai' with Moshe and later with Matisyahu.

title.en: The name Yisrael and tumah as a barrier

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Klal Yisrael carries the name Yisrael as a wife takes her husband's name, joining 'yashar' with Hashem's Name. Since Hashem is pure, the bond exists only with taharah; tumah is a barrier that destroys emunah, which is why so many mitzvos require taharah.

title.en: The Chazon Ish and the dentist's hands

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Chazon Ish, treated at night by a dentist who rushed over before washing his hands, felt the tumah of his fingers affect his learning. He adds that Torah must be learned in purity, and concludes that the war of Yavan was emunah against kefirah, tumah against taharah.

title.en: The Greeks in the Heichal and the hidden pach shemen

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Greeks entered the Heichal not to destroy but to defile, and that what is said of a woman applies to Klal Yisrael, who is pure. He asks how the pach shemen could be hidden under the Heichal floor without breaking its stones, answers from the Gemara in Sotah about a loose marble slab with a ring, from where the dust for the sotah was taken, and concludes that the pach symbolizes the purity of Knesses Yisrael.

title.en: Why Yaakov wanted the name Yisrael from the angel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yaakov wanted the angel of Esav to call him Yisrael rather than wait for Hashem at Beis El. He brings Rav Tzadok HaKohen that emunah includes knowing one is a Yisrael, the Radbaz that one may not even say he is a Yishmaeli in a time of persecution, and explains that Yaakov knew he would first face Shechem, which stands for the battle of Yehudis.

title.en: Shechem, Yavan and the separateness of Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shechem's idea, like Yavan's, was that the Jews are not separate, and that the Greeks forced Jews to write that they have no portion in the G-d of Yisrael. He brings 'ki nevalah asah b'Yisrael', the breaches the Greeks made in the barrier of the Temple Mount, and connects Chanukah to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael and to the mezuzah.

title.en: The war of tumah today

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that Yaakov needed the name Yisrael for his fight with Shechem, which stands for Yavan. He then says the war of Yavan is being replayed in the times before Moshiach through tumah brought into Jewish homes by electronic devices, mentions his shul's rule about cell phones, and calls for mesirus nefesh for taharah.

catalogTitle: ראש כל מועדות נשאת פסח; כנגד אברהם אבינו - חסד ואמונה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach, the head of all the festivals, is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, and therefore the Yom Tov of chesed, renewal and above all emunah, which a Jew takes in by eating matzah, the food of faith.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the three festivals corresponding to the three Avos: Pesach, the head of the festivals, belongs to Avraham, the root of Klal Yisrael. Only Pesach and milah carry kares for neglect, and kares shows that these mitzvos bind a Jew to Avraham and to his people. He then shows that Nissan is the month of chesed and the right side, while Tishrei is din, and that every Nissan the world is renewed: nature rises as if from the dead, and a Jew too must rise and renew his service. Avraham's quality is emunah, inherited by every Jew; at the Exodus the ten plagues revealed that Hashem created and runs the world. A story of souls sent down again and again leads to the lesson of complete trust in hashgacha pratis without saying 'would have'. Matzah, above time and place, is the food of emunah. He ends with preparing for Pesach through prayer, with stories, and with a tefillah for the final redemption.

en: Pesach is the head of the festivals because it corresponds to Avraham Avinu, the first point of Klal Yisrael, and it binds a Jew to his root.
The punishment of kares for neglecting Pesach and milah shows that these mitzvos are a bond, connecting a Jew to Avraham and to Klal Yisrael.
Nissan is a time of renewal in heaven that reaches down into nature, and a Jew is meant to renew himself spiritually and rise from his spiritual death.
Avraham's quality is emunah, inherited by every Jew, and the Exodus, seen by millions, is the foundation of the faith that is passed from generation to generation.
Emunah means trusting that everything comes from Hashem's personal providence, so a Jew should never say 'it would have been better'.
Matzah is the food of emunah: unlike chametz, which needs time and takes up space, it stands above time and place, as emunah does.

title.en: Pesach, head of the festivals, and Avraham

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three festivals correspond to the three Avos, with Pesach against Avraham, the root of the Avos and of Klal Yisrael, which makes it the head of the festivals. Shavuos and Sukkos have a higher holiness, but Pesach is the beginning and binds a Jew to his root.

title.en: Kares as a bond; Avraham's Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why only Pesach and milah carry kares, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim that kares shows the mitzvah is a bond, connecting a Jew to Avraham and to the nation. He then lists events of Avraham's life that took place on Pesach: the covenant, the milah, the matzah he baked and the war with the four kings.

title.en: Nissan, the month of chesed and the right side

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham is the attribute of chesed and the right side, which a Jew always puts first, and that Nissan is the month of the right side, whose name follows the alphabet in order, while Tishrei reverses it and is the month of din. With this he explains how the world was created in Tishrei in thought but in Nissan in deed.

title.en: Nissan renewal and techiyas hameisim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every festival repeats what happened originally, so every Nissan the world and the bond of Klal Yisrael are renewed. Nature in spring rises as if from the dead, the haftarah of Yechezkel's dry bones is read on Pesach, and a Jew must ask himself whether he too will rise and serve Hashem with life; even repainting the house and new clothes for Pesach express this renewal.

title.en: Avraham's emunah and the Exodus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Avraham's quality is emunah, which every Jew inherits, so Avraham's festival plants emunah. At the Exodus Hashem showed through the ten plagues, which correspond to the ten utterances of creation, that He created the world and runs it; this was seen by millions, as the Rambam writes, and is passed down from parent to child.

title.en: Seder night, the time to plant emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that the first of the Ten Commandments is emunah, rooted in the Exodus, and the Ohev Yisrael that the Seder night, when matzah and maror lie before us, is the time to tell the children about the Exodus and plant emunah in them. In the last generations, as the Gemara says of Chavakuk, everything rests on emunah alone.

title.en: The souls' complaint and 'would have'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story told by a disciple of the Ba'al Shem Tov: souls that kept failing and coming back complained until they reached Hashem, who advised them to rely on emunah alone, on one condition, never to say 'would have'. He illustrates with a brother who moved the alarm clock and a wife whose late breakfast cost a deal, and explains that 'would have' denies hashgacha pratis.

title.en: Emunah, the test of our time

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls emunah the soul of a Jew, the Avraham within him, and connects it with the blessing of Magen Avraham. He brings the Chofetz Chaim's words that there would be no more dybbuks, since now the test is to believe without seeing, and compares the questions of our generation to Avraham's test at the Akeidah.

title.en: Matzah, the food of emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that matzah is the food of faith, with an inner power like a vitamin or a pill. Everything in this world happens in time and place, while emunah is above both; chametz needs time and rises to take up space, but matzah does not. Bread is holy, three times the Name Havayah, but matzah equals three times the Name with its full spelling.

title.en: Praying for emunah; chametz and the yetzer hara

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a Jew must ask Hashem for complete emunah, which is the essence of his soul and for which even sinners gave their lives. He calls for preparing for Pesach in body and spirit, explaining with the Radvaz and the Zohar that the special strictness about chametz is because chametz is the yetzer hara, and ends with learning, davening and tzedakah before Pesach.

title.en: The tzaddik and the grain of wheat

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard from the Klausenburger Rav about a tzaddik who worked with great effort for a kosher Pesach and found a grain of wheat in his soup at the Seder. Asking in a dream, he was told that he had forgotten to pray to Hashem, and was shown how a bird dropped the grain down the chimney.

title.en: Salvation through the mitzvos of Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that without healthy emunah learning and davening are lacking, and that through the mitzvos of Pesach great salvations can be drawn down, which is why the Haggadah counts the plagues. He tells of the Ropshitzer's matzos against the Russians and Avraham's matzos against the four kings, urges davening and learning with life, tells of the Sanzer Rav's joy after the Seder, and closes with a prayer for the final Pesach in Yerushalayim.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Pesach as the level of yovel and the fiftieth gate, above the seven of Shabbos, and from it explains why Hillel alone knew that the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos, why David found the place of the Mikdash, and why Shlomo and Moshiach carry the light of the final redemption.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi's comment that the word 'im' by the omer and by yovel means an obligation, and with the Gemara's story of Hillel, who alone knew that the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos and was made Nasi. He sets beside it Doeg's envy of David for finding the place of the Mikdash. Using Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of world, year and soul, he explains that above the seven days of creation stands the level of 'pele', the fiftieth: yovel in time, the Mikdash in place, and the king in the soul. Pesach is the fiftieth gate, so it overrides Shabbos, which is only seven. David is Shabbos and Shlomo, his inner self, is yovel; Hillel is a gilgul of Shlomo, which is why he knew the halacha. The Mashgiach ends with Shir HaShirim's closing plea, the hard galus of Yishmael, and a call to daven on Pesach with emunah for the redemption.

en: Above the seven of Shabbos and shmitah stands the fiftieth, yovel, which is 'pele', beyond measure and understanding; Shavuos and Matan Torah, the Mikdash and Pesach all belong to it.
The place of the Mikdash is not named in the Torah because it is above 'place'; it must be sought, and only David, the 'reishis' and king of the soul, could find it.
Pesach is the fiftieth gate, which is why the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos, which is only the level of seven.
David is the seventh, Shabbos, while his inner depth, revealed in his son Shlomo who built the Mikdash, is yovel; Shlomo's era is a model of the days of Moshiach.
Hillel knew that Pesach overrides Shabbos because he is a gilgul of Shlomo, from the root of yovel, and not only because he had learned it from Shemaya and Avtalyon.
The Mashgiach says the days of Pesach are days of geulah and a time to daven, with emunah in Hashem alone, for the final redemption.
