title.en: 'Im' by the omer and by yovel

summary.en: During the days of the omer the Mashgiach cites Rashi that 've'im takriv' by the omer means an obligation, proven from 've'im yihyeh hayovel', and asks why the Torah uses 'im' by yovel. He then begins the Gemara's account of an Erev Pesach that fell on Shabbos, when the Bnei Beseira did not know whether the Pesach offering overrides Shabbos.

title.en: Hillel becomes Nasi

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Hillel ruled that Pesach overrides Shabbos, how the Bnei Beseira stepped down and made him Nasi, how he rebuked them and then forgot the law of carrying the knife until he saw what the people did. He brings the Rema MiPano that the kingship of Torah stayed with Hillel's family because he descends from David.

title.en: Doeg's envy and the three dimensions

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Zevachim that David and Shmuel determined the place of the Mikdash, and that Doeg, a greater scholar, envied David for it, which he likens to the Bnei Beseira and Hillel. He then brings Sefer Yetzirah that the world exists in place, time and soul, each with its 'king' and beginning, called 'pele'.

title.en: Above the seven: yovel and the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven days of creation and the middos from chesed to malchus have something above them: after shmitah comes yovel, after seven weeks of sefirah comes the fiftieth day, Shavuos and Matan Torah, 'bimshoch hayovel'. A slave whom the seventh year cannot free goes free at yovel, and Moshe added the fiftieth day because it is above reckoning.

title.en: The Mikdash, a place above place

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Beis HaMikdash is the place of yovel and 'pele': the Sanhedrin goes up there for a matter that is 'yipalei', and the Aron took up no space. Therefore the Torah gives no directions to the place of the Mikdash, only 'lishichno tidreshu', which he links by gematria to 'reishis'.

title.en: David, king of the soul, finds the Mikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the king is the 'pele' of the soul: even Shmuel did not know which son of Yishai was the king, just as the place of the Mikdash must be sought. Only David, the soul of Adam HaRishon and the 'reishis', could find the place, which answers Doeg's envy.

title.en: Pesach, the fiftieth gate

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nissan is the head of time and Pesach comes from the fiftieth gate, which Jews receive as a gift on the Seder night and then work toward through sefirah. He brings the Maharal on why Haman fell on the first day of the omer, and explains that Pesach is yovel and therefore overrides Shabbos.

title.en: David is Shabbos, Shlomo is yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach links Rosh Chodesh Nissan to the Kodesh HaKodashim and to 'kinas beischa'. He brings Rav Tzadok HaKohen that a father's inner self is revealed in his son: David is the seventh, Shabbos, and his inner depth, yovel, came out in Shlomo, who built the Mikdash and whose reign the Rambam's picture of Moshiach resembles.

title.en: Hillel, Shlomo, and the fiftieth Exodus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that Moshiach must come from Shlomo, and the Rema MiPano that Hillel is a gilgul of Shlomo. He asks why the Seder expounds 'Arami oved avi' and answers that the fiftieth mention of the Exodus, belonging to the days of Moshiach, is there; therefore Pesach overrides Shabbos, and the Bnei Beseira could not know it.

title.en: Hillel's ruling from the root of his soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Seder night is a time of asking without knowing, and that Hillel's ruling revealed the fiftieth gate because he is Shlomo, so the kingdom was set in his hand. Hillel credited Shemaya and Avtalyon out of humility, so Heaven made him forget the knife, revealing that his knowledge came from his soul's root. This also explains 'im' by the omer and yovel.

title.en: Shir HaShirim's last plea and Har HaMoriah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the days of Pesach are days of geulah, when a Jew must long for redemption. Shlomo ends Shir HaShirim with 'berach dodi', a plea that Hashem flee the galus with His people to Har HaMoriah. Yet today Yishmael holds that place, and he brings the Chasam Sofer that korbanos cannot be offered because Yishmael will not let a Jew go up.

title.en: The galus of Yishmael, 'pere adam'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam's Igeres Teiman that no galus is harder than that of Yishmael, from 'oyah li' in Tehillim, and that Yishmael hates peace. He brings Rav Chaim Vital that 'bekum aleinu adam' refers to Yishmael, the 'pere adam', and the Chofetz Chaim's warning that a Yishmaeli remains a 'pere adam' whatever he becomes.

title.en: 'Adam velo melech'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the same passuk refers to Haman, 'adam velo melech', and the Bnei Yissaschar that the seven nations parallel the seven middos and the Girgashi, as malchus, accepted Hashem's kingship and left. Achashverosh as a king had a spark of malchus, Haman did not; Yishmael too has only princes and no king, which makes his galus so hard.

title.en: Only Hashem can help: davening on Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yishmael is the impure side of yesod, a Friday that never reaches Shabbos, and that only Hashem can save from him, not politics or the military. Pesach, a time of revealed Shechinah, is the time to daven with emunah in Hashem and in tzaddikim for the redemption and for 'berach dodi'.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to children, the Mashgiach explains that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first believer, and that its matzah and its 'great wealth' are emunah in Hashem.

abstract.en: Addressing children, the Mashgiach opens by calling Pesach the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu: Avraham was the first Jew, Pesach is the first Yom Tov of the year, and Avraham is the one figure in the Torah of whom it is written that he ate matzos. He was also the first of whom the Torah says that he believed in Hashem. Since matzah is called the food of emunah, eating it with joy plants emunah in a Jew for the whole year. The Mashgiach describes that emunah: Hashem stands over a person and sees and knows everything he does, says and thinks, so how could he sin; Hashem can do everything, so one may rely on Him and not worry. He then shows how Avraham's own life ran on Pesach, and how the 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is, for every Jew, emunah. He closes with the coming Pesach of the future, when Moshiach will say he came because of the children who learned, davened and kept away from aveiros.

en: Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu: he was the first Jew, Pesach is the first Yom Tov, and he is the one tzaddik in the Torah of whom it says he ate matzos.
Matzah is the food of emunah; eating it with joy gives a Jew emunah for the whole year.
Emunah means believing that Hashem stands over a person and sees everything he does, says and thinks, which keeps him from sin.
Since Hashem can do everything, a Jew can rely on Him and need not worry about what he needs.
The 'great wealth' with which Jews leave Pesach is emunah, the greatest treasure a Jew owns.
In the future redemption Moshiach will say that he came because of the children who learned Torah, davened and kept away from aveiros.

title.en: Pesach, matzah and Avraham's emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the children that Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, the first Jew and the first in the Torah who believed in Hashem and ate matzos. Since matzah is the food of emunah, eating it with joy gives emunah for the whole year.

title.en: Hashem stands over us; the true great wealth

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that emunah means knowing Hashem sees everything and can do everything, so one keeps from sin and relies on Him. He shows how Avraham's life ran on Pesach and that the 'great wealth' promised to Avraham is, for every Jew, emunah.

title.en: The great Pesach of the future

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the future Pesach when Hashem will gather Jews from every land, ties it to the haftarah of the dry bones, and says Moshiach will credit the children who learned, davened and avoided aveiros. He closes by urging joy and emunah through the rest of Pesach.
